nodes.title: Posterior Cord Syndrome
nodes.body:
• Etiology: Vitamin B12 deficiency, Syphilis (Tabes dorsalis), thyroid Dx, Copper deficiency, zinc toxicity, PSA (posterior spinal artery) compression, e.g. tumor, or iatrogenic from spinal surgery (accessed posteriorly)
  • Intact: motor + pain/temp
  • Lose: vibration + proprioception at all levels below lesion
    • pt presents w. unsteadiness + paresthesias
  • → Sensory ataxia w. positive Romberg sign (see Ataxia DDx on right side of map)

nodes.title: Anterior Cord Syndrome
nodes.body:
• Etiology: anterior spinal artery pathology, e.g. ASA atherosclerosis or aneurysm, or ASA compression, e.g. herniated disc
  • Intact: vibration/proprioception
  • Lose: motor + pain/temp at all levels below lesion
    • pt presents w. quadri/paraplegia + paresthesias

nodes.title: Central Cord Syndrome
nodes.body:
• (Most common syndrome)
  • Etiology: elderly falls (spinal hyperextension injury), intrinsic tumors, syrinx (central CSF cyst), demyelinating Dx (MS)
  • Intact: vibration/proprioception
  • Lose: pain/temp only at the same level of lesion (suspended sensory loss) ⭐
  • Motor loss mainly in distal muscles (related to the somatotopic organization of the corticospinal tract)

nodes.title: Dorsal Column
nodes.body:
• Vibration + proprioception
  • ⭐ Large nerve fibres (myelinated): faster than pain + temp
  • Both DCML + spinothalamic tract carry light touch sensation
  • Fasciculus gracilis (medial): lower limb, sensory below T6
  • Fasciculus cuneatus (lateral): upper limb, sensory above T6
  • Decussation: ascends in posterior cord, decussates at medulla

nodes.title: Lateral Corticospinal Tract
nodes.body:
• Somatic motor to limbs
  • Anterior corticospinal tract carries motor to axial/trunk for posture + balance
  • Decussation: ascends in anterior-lateral cord, decussates at medulla (pyramids)

nodes.title: Spinothalamic Tract
nodes.body:
• Pain + temperature
  • Small nerve fibres (unmyelinated): slower than vibration/proprioception
  • Decussation: crosses via the anterior white commissure at the spinal cord, at the same level it enters the cord; ascends in anterior cord

nodes.title: Brown-Séquard Syndrome
nodes.body:
• aka hemicord syndrome
  • Etiology: trauma or intrinsic cord Dx; usually an incomplete lesion
  • Lose: ipsilateral motor and vibration/proprioception; contralateral pain/temp ❗⭐
  • All tracts lost at all levels below lesion

nodes.title: Spinal Cord Tracts
nodes.body:
• Lesions present as syndromes
  • Drawing: cord cross-section with tracts coloured; lateral corticospinal tract labelled S L T C (somatotopic layers)
  • Ventral/anterior (ASA supply):
    • Spinothalamic tract → crosses over at the same spine level ∴ contralateral s/s ⭐
    • Spinocerebellar tract → crosses over twice ∴ ipsilateral
    • Corticospinal tract → crosses at medulla (bracketed with the dorsal tracts below)
  • Dorsal/posterior (PSA supply): fasciculus gracilis, fasciculus cuneatus
    • Corticospinal + gracilis + cuneatus → cross over at medulla (brainstem) ∴ ipsilateral s/s ⭐
  • Note: anterior and posterior spinal cord have different blood supply:
    • Subclavian A → vertebral arteries → basilar A → anterior spinal A (ASA)
    • Vertebral arteries → posterior inferior cerebellar A → posterior spinal A (PSA)

nodes.title: Spinal Cord 📍
nodes.body:
• (Cervical + thoracic myelopathy)
  • UMN if lesions above L1:
    • spinal cord ends at L1 (conus medullaris); below that the cord continues as lumbar + sacral roots (cauda equina)
    • so L2-S5 lesions present w. LMN findings
  • Typically presents with:
    • Bladder + bowel deficits: descending PSNS fibres ⭐ (exit at S2-S4 level ∴ also present in cauda equina syndrome)
    • Hemi/quadri/para-plegia/paresis: corticospinal tract
    • Hemi/quadri/para-sensory deficits / sensory level: dorsal columns (touch, vibration, proprioception); spinothalamic tract (pain, temp)
  • Estimating the sensory level (highest level of abnormal sensation on pin prick / highest level of UMN s/s) estimates the level of lesion
    • order MRI in both axial and sagittal view at the estimated level of SC lesion
  • A truncal sensory level is very specific for thoracic myelopathy ❗

nodes.title: Quadriplegia & Paraplegia
nodes.body:
• (or quadriparesis + paraparesis)
  • PEx: UMN/pyramidal
  • Complete cervical cord lesion: quadriplegia/paresis
  • Complete thoracic cord lesion: paraplegia/paresis
  • + no sensory function below level of lesion, loss of rectal tone + urinary incontinence

nodes.title: Hemiplegia (or Hemiparesis)
nodes.body:
• PEx: UMN/pyramidal
  • Lesion in motor cortex, tracts or spinal cord:
    • Face/arm > leg weakness: MCA region (lateral homunculus)
    • Leg > face/arm weakness: ACA region (medial homunculus)
      • face + limb s/s on the same body side (contralateral to side of lesion)
    • Face/arm = leg weakness: internal capsule, brainstem (face + limb s/s on "crossed" sides)
    • Arm + leg weakness (no face s/s) w. spinal cord s/s (bladder, sensory level): partial spinal cord lesion

nodes.title: Common presentation: MCA Stroke
nodes.body:
• Face + arm > leg hemiparesis
  • Aphasia: read the CT carefully for R/L, since mainly a LEFT MCA stroke would cause aphasia

nodes.title: Aphasia
nodes.body:
• Impairment of language, vs. dysarthria, which is an impairment of articulation
  • Language PEx: comprehension, naming, repetition, fluency

nodes.title: Apraxia
nodes.body:
• Inability to carry out a motor task despite having the power to do so
  • e.g. dressing apraxia

nodes.title: Syndromes of the Dominant Hemisphere
nodes.body: • (Typically LEFT if right-handed)

nodes.title: Syndromes of the Non-Dominant Hemisphere
nodes.body: • (Typically RIGHT if right-handed)

nodes.title: Syndromes of the Cortical Sensory Areas
Cerebral Cortex 📍
nodes.body:
• Typically presents with:
    • hemiparesis: 1° motor cortex (frontal lobe)
    • hemisensory deficits: 1° somatosensory deficits (parietal lobe)
    • aphasia (if left hemisphere), neglect (if right hemisphere)
    • cognitive deficits

nodes.title: Subcortical Lesions: Cerebral White Matter Tracts
nodes.body:
• (Corona radiata, internal capsule, corpus callosum...)
  • Internal capsule key fibres:
    • leg, arm + face: pure sensory } lesions can affect either one or both
    • leg, arm + face: pure motor }
    • cerebellar fibres (∴ hemibody ataxia w. hemibody hemiparesis)

nodes.title: UMN Lesion (Upper Motor Neuron, CNS)
nodes.body:
• PEx findings (pyramidal signs):
    • Bulk: normal (no significant atrophy) + no fasciculations
    • Tone: ↑ tone (velocity dependent = spasticity, or velocity independent = rigidity)
      • in children: hypotonia (evolves to hypertonicity by 2-3 y.o.)
    • Reflexes: hyperreflexia (grade 3-4) due to ↓ inhibition of reflexes in spinal cord → clonus (rhythmic contractions) in response to sudden muscle stretching
  • Special tests for UMN lesion:
    • Plantar reflexes: extensor (upgoing; up = bad) plantar response, aka Babinski sign
      • in hands may exhibit Hoffmann's sign (flexion of thumb/index when flicking nail of middle finger)
    • Pattern of weakness: pyramidal pattern, weaker leg flexors, arm extensors and forearm supinators (contributes to pronator drift w. UMN lesions)
  • Invx + diagnosis: clinical and imaging via MRI or CT

nodes.title: Brainstem 📍
nodes.body:
• S/s related to key structures in brainstem: cranial nerve nuclei
    • Midbrain: CN III + IV (vulnerable to herniation, aneurysms + trauma): diplopia + ptosis
    • Pons: CN V, VI, VII, VIII (vulnerable to basilar A pathology): facial sensory deficits, facial droop, vertigo
    • Medulla: CN IX, X, XI, XII (basilar A pathology): dysarthria, dysphagia
    • Descending SNS fibres: Horner's syndrome
    • } all of the above innervate the ipsilateral face
  • Cerebellar tracts/peduncles: ataxia
  • Corticospinal tract/pyramids (ventral): hemiparesis
  • Spinothalamic tract + DCML, fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus (dorsal): sensory deficits
  • } these three innervate the contralateral body

nodes.title: Pons Lesion
nodes.body:
• Contains CN V, VI, VII, VIII nuclei
  • Facial sensory deficits, facial droop, vertigo + other s/s listed under "Brainstem"
  • e.g. locked-in syndrome if severe bilateral lesion (CN III, IV maintained: can move eyes up + down)
  • e.g. due to occlusion of basilar A (stroke): basilar thrombosis
  • Tx: thrombolytics (tPA)

nodes.title: Lesions in both Pons & Medulla present w. "Crossed" Sensory S/S
nodes.body:
• Lesion is ipsilateral to face s/s: the trigeminal tract (CN V) descends ipsilaterally through the pons + medulla
  • Lesion is contralateral to limb/body s/s: ascending spinal tracts decussated in the caudal pyramids or spinal cord

nodes.title: Medullary Lesion
nodes.body:
• aka bulbar lesion
  • Contains CN IX, X, XI, XII nuclei
  • e.g. lateral medullary syndrome
  • CN IX, X, XII innervate pharynx + larynx (bulbar muscles), which mediate phonation + swallowing ∴ lesions present w. dysarthria + dysphagia + s/s listed under "Brainstem"
  • Also houses the cardiorespiratory centre ∴ may present w. dyspnea
  • If severe lesion (tonsillar herniation): Cushing's triad (bradycardia, hypertension, apnea)

nodes.title: Lower CNs (IX, X, XI, XII) note
nodes.body: • May also be affected by intracranial base of skull Dx: meningioma, metastases, meningitis, osteomyelitis...

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Weakness
nodes.body:
• (Muscle power <5 on PEx)
  • Begin DDx w. Hx and PEx for UMN or LMN lesion signs

nodes.title: Localization
nodes.body: • Method shown w. HPI of weakness, but a similar approach is used for HPI of abnormal sensation

nodes.title: Weakness Mimics
nodes.body:
• Ataxia (cerebellar Dx)
  • Apraxia (cerebral Dx)
  • Severe sensory loss (e.g. proprioceptive failure)

nodes.title: LMN Lesion (Lower motor neuron: PNS and spinal cord lesions below L1 level)
nodes.body:
• PEx findings:
    • Bulk: muscle atrophy and fasciculations may be seen
    • Tone: normal or hypotonia (flaccid muscles)
    • Reflexes: normal, hyporeflexia or areflexia (grade 0-2)
    • Plantar reflexes: flexor (downgoing) or absent (normal)
    • Pattern of weakness: proximal (shoulder/hip), myotomal, distal (feet → knees → hands), focal (single nerve), ocular... depends on lesion
  • Invx + diagnosis: often clinical or via EMG/NCS

nodes.title: Motor and Sensory Deficits
nodes.body: • Analyze the pattern of distribution (locations): pattern of weakness and sensory deficits

nodes.title: Spinal Nerve/Root 📍
nodes.body:
• Includes L2-S5 spine lesions ⭐
  • aka radiculopathy
  • Usually asymmetrical (one arm or leg)
  • Neck (C1-C8) or low back (L1-S5) pain
  • Radiating pain + paresthesia in dermatome (arm/leg), weakness in myotome w. LMN pattern
  • Common lesions (e.g. due to disc herniation):
    • C6 radiculopathy (vs. carpal tunnel)
    • C8 radiculopathy: site of SNS fibre exit, may be associated w. Horner syndrome
      • C8 most responsible for hand dexterity
    • L5 or S1 radiculopathy: low back + leg pain
      • L5 w. foot drop + weak inversion
      • S1 w. weak plantarflexion (toe walk)
    • (See MSK Anki for full review)

nodes.title: Polyradiculopathy
nodes.body:
• Multiple spinal nerves/roots, lesion outside spinal canal
  • Presents as multiple radiculopathies

nodes.title: Mild Lumbar Stenosis → Neurogenic Claudication
nodes.body: • Neurogenic claudication: PEx bilateral s/s resembling polyradiculopathy where pain worsens w. exercise + back/hip extension but improves w. forward flexion (hip/back)

nodes.title: Severe Lumbar Stenosis → Cauda Equina Syndrome
nodes.body:
• Clinical presentation:
    • Motor fibres: paraparesis w. LMN pattern
    • Sensory fibres: bilateral leg pain + paresthesia, e.g. at the S2-S4 dermatome → saddle anesthesia
    • PSNS fibres (S2-S4): impaired bladder + bowel control ❗
  • Management: URGENT MRI and referral for emergency spinal surgery

nodes.title: Dorsal Root Ganglion 📍
nodes.body:
• e.g. post-herpetic neuralgia
    • shingles (varicella zoster reactivation in DRG) → vesicles and neuropathic pain along dermatome
  • Other sensory neuronopathies:
    • trigeminal neuralgia
    • paraneoplastic, autoimmune (Sjögren's), toxic (↑B6, cisplatin)

nodes.title: Nerve Plexus 📍
nodes.body:
• Single limb, affected muscles are innervated by various nerves/roots
  • e.g. Erb's or Klumpke's palsy

nodes.title: Asymmetrical Distribution → Mononeuropathy
nodes.body:
• Mononeuropathy: weakness and abnormal sensation along a single nerve distribution (aka focal)
  • Common lesions (anatomically vulnerable nerves):
    • Carpal tunnel syndrome: median N palsy (vs. C6 radiculopathy; distinguish via dermatome PEx: C6 affects forearm)
    • Foot drop: common or deep peroneal N palsy (vs. L5 radiculopathy; distinguish via inversion, only affected w. L5 rad, which is also typically more painful, otherwise ↓ power)
    • Dyspnea: phrenic N neuropathy (DDx w. resp + heart Dx); worse supine, better upright
    • Others: ulnar, radial, sciatic N palsies
  • Invx: EMG to confirm Dx
  • Lesions via 3 main mechanisms → Neurotmesis, Axonotmesis, Neurapraxia

nodes.title: Neurotmesis
nodes.body:
• Nerve cut or laceration (e.g. trauma)
  • Injury to axon and epineurium
  • Tx: does not self-resolve; surgery and potential nerve graft

nodes.title: Axonotmesis
nodes.body:
• Wallerian degeneration (e.g. nerve crush/stretch, ischemia due to vasculitis, toxic insults)
  • Injury to axon but intact epineurium
  • Tx: self-resolves via Wallerian regeneration, but slow (1 inch per month)

nodes.title: Neurapraxia
nodes.body:
• Transient functional block (e.g. lidocaine, hypothermia) or nerve compression
  • Injury to myelin, intact axon
  • Tx: self-resolves (re-myelination) in hours to 3 months

nodes.title: Mononeuropathy Multiplex
nodes.body:
• Multiple mononeuropathies
  • Asymmetric polyneuropathy
  • Etiology: vasculitis, ischemia affecting multiple individual nerves...

nodes.title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)
nodes.body:
• aka acute inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy (AIDP)
  • Pathophys: infection (URTI or GI, e.g. food poisoning w. Campylobacter jejuni) → antigen mimicry ↑ autoantibodies → 2-3 weeks post-infection: autoimmune destruction of myelin of peripheral nerves (not CNS)
  • Clinical presentation:
    • often motor deficits occur first + are most prominent
    • symmetrical ascending paralysis (starts in legs), areflexia/hyporeflexia, distal paresthesias + neuropathic pain
    • progression to more proximal nerves is fast (days): risk of imminent respiratory failure (may need intubation)
  • Invx: EMG/NCS (shows slowing, motor > sensory); lumbar puncture (CSF w. ↑ protein, normal WBC)
  • Tx: IVIG and plasmapheresis (no steroids)

nodes.title: Other Etiologies (demyelinating)
nodes.body:
• Diphtheria toxin
  • CIDP (chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy)
  • Hereditary

nodes.title: Length-Dependent Polyneuropathy
nodes.body:
• aka "distal dying back" or "peripheral neuropathy"
  • Pathophys: axonal transport issues → degeneration of distal portion of axons, progressing proximally (ascending)
    • longest nerves in the body are affected first → slowly (years) + progressively affects shorter nerves
  • Clinical presentation:
    • often sensory deficits occur first + are most prominent: sensory (neuropathic pain) → motor (weakness) + autonomic (orthostatic hypotension, urinary + GI s/s)
    • pattern of sensory deficits: ↓ sensation or pain in both feet (stocking) → knees → hands/fingers (glove) ❗
    • pattern of weakness is the same: symmetrical + distal muscle weakness (feet, ankles) first, then progresses more proximally
  • Etiology:
    • Others: renal failure + uremia; hypothyroidism, Vit B12 def; infectious (HIV, leprosy...); drugs + chemotherapy (vincristine, cisplatin, metronidazole); toxins/heavy metals (lead, arsenic...); autoimmune or hereditary

nodes.title: Diabetic Neuropathy
nodes.body:
• Most common cause, often presents as burning feet
  • Tx: neuropathic pain meds; glycemic control to prevent worsening Dx (note that existing damage is not reversible)

nodes.title: Length-Dependent Sensory Neuropathies
nodes.body: • Can be further classified as large vs small fibre

nodes.title: Large Fiber (myelinated)
nodes.body:
• Carry vibration, proprioception, Golgi tendon for reflexes (to DCML)
  • PEx: numb feet, paresthesias, poor balance
  • ↓ afferent reflex fibres → hyporeflexia, absent ankle jerks
  • (Detected via EMG/NCS)

nodes.title: Small Fiber (mixed un/myelinated)
nodes.body:
• Carry pain (pin prick) + temperature (to spinothalamic tract)
  • PEx: burning feet, dysesthesias, hyperpathia
  • (too small to detect via EMG/NCS)
  • Most commonly caused by diabetic neuropathy

nodes.title: Neuropathic Pain
nodes.body:
• (Pain due to CNS or PNS lesion)
  • Allodynia, hyperpathia, dysesthesia (e.g. paresthesia, burning, electrical...)
  • Peripheral causes: length-dependent neuropathy, mononeuropathy, radiculopathy, shingles...
  • Central causes: lesions to sensory tracts on thalamus, brainstem, spinal cord
  • Treatment (does NOT usually respond to NSAIDs):
    • Antidepressants:
      • TCAs (amitriptyline) if co-morbid sleep disorder; also the cheapest option
      • SNRIs (duloxetine) if co-morbid depression
    • Anticonvulsants: gabapentin, pregabalin
    • Topical: capsaicin, lidocaine gel/patch
    • Others: cannabinoids, narcotics (last resort)

nodes.title: Nociceptive Pain
nodes.body:
• Somatic or visceral pain from tissues
  • Treatment: acetaminophen, NSAIDs, opioids

nodes.title: Complex Regional Pain Syndromes (CRPS)
nodes.body:
• Tissue or nerve injury ± peripheral/central sensitization → pain greater + lasting longer than expected ∴ chronic pain w. inflammatory + autonomic features:
    • pain, allodynia, swelling, skin temp/colour changes, hair + nail changes...
  • Complex and multidisciplinary Tx

nodes.title: Muscles (Myopathy) 📍
nodes.body:
• PEx: symmetrical and proximal muscle weakness (neck, shoulders, hip) w. normal sensation, and often normal reflexes
  • Etiology: muscular dystrophy, polymyositis/dermatomyositis; could be 1° or 2°, e.g. cancer immunotherapy (review PoM II rheumatology map)
  • Invx: serum creatine kinase ❗ + EMG/NCS, and Invx for other causes of myopathic weakness:
    • thyroid Dx (Invx w. TSH)
    • electrolyte disturbance (Invx w. Na+, Ca2+, Mg)

nodes.title: Anterior Horn Cells (Motor Neuronopathies) 📍
nodes.body:
• Other etiologies:
    • post-polio and polio-like Dx (acute asymmetric descending paralysis)
    • West Nile

nodes.title: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
nodes.body:
• aka Lou Gehrig's disease
  • Pathophys: idiopathic (most) or genetic → progressive degeneration of motor neurons in the brain (UMN) and anterior horn of spinal cord (LMN)
  • PEx: asymmetric + segmental weakness w. mixed UMN/LMN s/s in at least 2 regions; progressively spreads to other regions
    • often starts as hand weakness, foot drop, dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue atrophy and fasciculations
    • no sensory or coordination issues; sparing of bladder + bowel
  • Invx: EMG/NCS, MRI, CSF... to rule out other Dx: diagnosis of exclusion
  • Tx: no cure as of 2024; supportive Tx w. BiPAP and multidisciplinary team; progression slowed w. riluzole + edaravone
  • Prognosis: death on average 3 yrs after onset

nodes.title: Neuromuscular Junction 📍
nodes.body: • Others: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, botulism...

nodes.title: Myasthenia Gravis
nodes.body:
• Pathophys: acquired autoimmunity (unknown MOA) or thymus Dx (e.g. thymoma) → IgG autoantibodies to skeletal muscle acetylcholine receptors (AChR) or MuSK
    • → blockade of ACh binding + ↑ degradation of AChR: ↓ AChR function (synaptic rundown) → muscle fatigability + weakness
  • PEx: fluctuating weakness ❗ (muscles fatigue) that worsens w. activity + through the day + improves w. rest
  • Descending weakness (arrow down):
    • ocular muscles affected 1st: diplopia, ptosis are the 1st s/s ❗⭐
    • bulbar muscles (CN IX, X, XII): dysphagia + dysarthria
    • respiratory muscles: dyspnea → limbs: proximal muscles
  • Reflexes tend to be normal; normal sensation
  • Invx: AChR autoantibodies, EMG/NCS, chest CT
  • Tx: AChE inhibitors, steroids, IVIG if myasthenic crisis

nodes.title: Classifications of Cerebral Palsy
nodes.body:
• Spastic (most common): ↑ tone, ↑ reflex, clonus
    • lesion to cortex; subclassified by limbs affected: hemiplegia, diplegia or quadriplegia (↑ risk of intellectual disability)
  • Dyskinetic: athetosis ± chorea or ↓ tone; lesion to basal ganglia
  • Ataxic: ataxic gait ± intention tremor; lesion to cerebellum
  • Mixed: 2+ of the above

nodes.title: Cerebral Palsy
nodes.body:
• Non-progressive central motor impairment syndrome due to CNS anomaly or neural injury at the prenatal, perinatal or postnatal stage
  • Diagnosed after age 2 y.o.: children w. motor s/s will either outgrow them/resolve or evolve to a clear CP pattern as they grow older (often by 2 y.o.)
  • GMFCS (level 1-5) and MACS: scales to estimate functional limitations

nodes.title: Genetic
nodes.body:
• Prader-Willi syndrome
  • Down syndrome
  • Fragile X syndrome
  • Trisomy 13 and 18

nodes.title: Pre/Perinatal
nodes.body:
• Intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), e.g. due to prematurity, birth trauma...
  • Hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), e.g. due to placental abruption, umbilical cord prolapse/compression, fetal anemia, pre-eclampsia...
  • Vascular (e.g. stroke) or other CNS malformations

nodes.title: UMN Lesion (infant)
nodes.body:
• (More common than LMN)
  • PEx: ↑ deep tendon reflexes and clonus, floppy truncal (axial) hypotonia, and strong; +ve Babinski; neonatal reflexes present ± seizures, fisted hands

nodes.title: Hypotonia aka "Floppy Infant" Syndrome
nodes.body:
• PEx w. traction response, axillary suspension + ventral suspension (baby hangs loose when held/carried by arms/armpits/belly)
  • In children <3 y.o. both UMN and LMN lesions present w. hypotonia, vs. in children >3 y.o. and adults only LMN lesions present w. hypotonia
    • ∴ hypotonia evolves to hypertonicity by 2-3 y.o. if central/UMN lesion

nodes.title: Mixed UMN/LMN Etiologies
nodes.body:
• Mitochondrial disorders (↑ CSF/blood lactate)
  • Storage diseases (e.g. Tay-Sachs)
  • Leukodystrophy

nodes.title: Non-Neurologic Etiologies
nodes.body:
• (Most common cause of hypotonia)
  • Metabolic: hypoglycemia, kernicterus
  • Endocrine: hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism
  • Systemic: TORCH infection, sepsis, dehydration
  • Most common cause of floppy infants is 2° to infections ❗
    • Invx: electrolytes, glucose, ABGs, CK...

nodes.title: LMN Lesion (infant)
nodes.body:
• PEx: ↓ or lack of deep tendon reflexes; floppy, truncal/axial and appendicular hypotonia, and weak; -ve Babinski; neonatal reflexes absent
  • Often w. FHx of neuromuscular Dx
  • Invx: serum CK, EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy

nodes.title: LMN Lesion Etiologies (infant)
nodes.body:
• Peripheral nerve:
    • Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease: demyelination + axonal injury; more common than GBS in children
  • Muscle:
    • Congenital muscular dystrophies (issues w. extracellular structures, e.g. collagen, laminin)
    • Congenital myopathies (issues w. intracellular components of muscle cells)
    • Congenital myotonic dystrophy (triple nucleotide repeat disorder: CTG repeat >1000)
      • PEx: severe hypotonia, facial weakness w. ptosis, respiratory and cardiac deficits, intellectual disability
      • ❗ Examine mother for s/s of classic myotonic dystrophy, e.g. myotonia (failure to relax muscles), e.g. difficulty relaxing grip (dashed → Classic Myotonic Dystrophy)
      • Invx mother for myotonic dystrophy w. EMG/NCS
  • Anterior horn cell:
    • less common Dx: polio, amyoplasia
    • spinal muscular atrophy (equivalent to ALS in adults); SMN gene on 5q13, unclear pathophys
  • NMJ:
    • transient (<5 wks) myasthenia gravis
    • congenital myasthenic syndromes (Invx: gene panels)
    • botulism (e.g. honey)

nodes.title: Classic Myotonic Dystrophy
nodes.body:
• CTG repeats 100-1,000; onset age 10-30 y.o.
  • PEx: weakness, myotonia, cataracts, balding, arrhythmia, chronic fatigue
  • Autosomal dominant Dx w. anticipation (similar to Huntington's)

nodes.title: CNs V, VI, VII, VIII
nodes.body: • Section label bracketing the V-VIII nerve nodes

nodes.title: Face
nodes.body:
• Motor via VII + V3
  • Sensory via V1, V2, V3

nodes.title: Mandibular N. (V3) branch diagram
nodes.body:
• (Motor) → Muscles of Mastication
    • (Gen. sensory) → Inf. Alveolar N. → Mental N.
    • → Buccal N.
    • → Lingual N. (gen. sens., blue) → Tongue ant 2/3. Chorda tympani joins it, carrying taste (purple) + PSNS (green).
    • → Auriculotemporal N. (gen. sensory anterior to ear) → Parotid gland (PSNS route)

nodes.title: Muscles of Mastication
nodes.body:
• Masseter
  • Temporalis

nodes.title: Tongue
nodes.body:
• Ant 2/3: CN V3, VII
  • Post 1/3: CN IX
  • Motor via CN XII

nodes.title: Untreated OM Complications
nodes.body: • ex. meningitis, intracranial abscess, Bell's palsy (rarely)

nodes.title: CN VII: Facial N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers:
    • Motor: facial expression + corneal reflex motor
    • S. sensory: taste from ant 2/3 tongue (purple asterisk)
    • PSNS: glands (tears, saliva)
  • Cell bodies (nucleus): pons (motor neurons)
  • Foramina: int. acoustic meatus into petrous part of temporal bone; exits via stylomastoid foramen
  • Cell bodies (ganglia): PSNS post-synap. in SUBMANDIBULAR + PTERYGOPALATINE GANGLIA

nodes.title: Facial N. (in petrous part of temporal bone)
nodes.body: • Facial N. in petrous part of temporal bone; dashed circle = near middle ear

nodes.title: Nerve to Stapedius
nodes.body: • Dampens loud sounds

nodes.title: Muscles of Facial Expression
nodes.body:
• Orbicularis oculi → BLINKING/closing eye via CN VII ∴ Bell's palsy: can't blink (open eyes while sleeping)
    • VS opening eye due to upper eyelid (LPS), mainly via CN III (some SNS) ∴ CN III palsy: ptosis (drooped eyelid)
  • Orbicularis oris
  • Zygomaticus major
  • Buccinator
  • Platysma
  • Frontalis & occipitalis → FOREHEAD HAS BILATERAL UMN INNERVATION

nodes.title: Forehead Has Bilateral UMN Innervation
nodes.body:
• Diagram key: blue = lower face, red = forehead; CN VII nucleus marked; lesion sites 1 and 2
  • 1: UMN lesion spares forehead (can weakly close ipsilateral eye but can't "bury eyelashes")
  • 2: LMN lesion affects forehead (cannot close ipsilateral eye, but globe rotates up to protect cornea)

nodes.title: Bell's Palsy
nodes.body:
• Idiopathic LMN facial neuropathy
  • Or CN lesion due to PAROTID GLAND TUMOR or SWELLING from infection
  • PEx: ipsilateral facial droop, ↓ blinking (+ dry eyes), ↓ ant 2/3 taste, ↑ sound (↓ dampening from stapedius)

nodes.title: CN IX: Glossopharyngeal N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers:
    • PSNS: parotid gland
    • Spec. sens: taste to post 1/3 tongue (purple asterisk)
    • Gen. sens: post 1/3 tongue, oropharynx + palate + gag reflex sens.
    • Motor: stylopharyngeus
  • Cell bodies (nucleus): medulla (motor)
  • Foramina: jugular foramen
  • Cell bodies (ganglia): PSNS post-syn. in OTIC GANGLION

nodes.title: Vagus Nerve
nodes.body:
• ∴ Test CN X via gag reflex if non-responsive, or ask pt. to "say aaah" and look inside:
    • CN X: palate elevation (PEx w. DEVIATED PALATE)
    • CN X: phonation (PEx w. DYSARTHRIA and/or HOARSENESS)

nodes.title: CN X: Vagus N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers:
    • Motor: palate, pharynx + gag reflex motor + larynx (phonation via recurrents)
    • Gen. sens: laryngopharynx & larynx
    • PSNS: thoracic & abdominal viscera
  • Cell bodies (nucleus): medulla (motor)
  • Foramina: jugular foramen
  • Cell bodies (ganglia): PSNS post-synap. in VISCERAL GANGLIA

nodes.title: CN XI: Accessory N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers: motor: trapezius, SCM
  • Cell bodies (nucleus): medulla
  • Foramina: in via foramen magnum, out via jugular foramen

nodes.title: CN XII: Hypoglossal N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers: motor: tongue
  • Cell bodies (nucleus): medulla
  • Foramina: hypoglossal canal

nodes.title: CN XII Lesion PEx
nodes.body:
• TONGUE DEVIATION towards the IPSILATERAL side of CN lesion
  • LMN lesions also present w. TONGUE ATROPHY + FASCICULATIONS
  • Lisp of speech, difficulty moving food

nodes.title: See Clinical Approach to Ptosis
nodes.body: • (CN III palsy, Horner's syndrome)

nodes.title: Why Are Ocular Muscles Affected First?
nodes.body:
• NMJ transmission also affected by temperature; more EFFICIENT in the COLD
  • Head is one of the warmest body regions → earlier impairment of NMJ transmission

nodes.title: Sensitization
nodes.body: • ↑ responsiveness of sensory neurons (if nociceptive neurons: ↑ pain)

nodes.title: CN VIII: Vestibulocochlear N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers: S. sensory: hearing, balance, VOR
  • Cell bodies: vestibular + cochlear ganglia and interneurons in PONS of BRAINSTEM
  • Foramina: int. acoustic meatus

nodes.title: Cochlea
nodes.body: • Hearing; lesions cause TINNITUS + HEARING LOSS

nodes.title: Conductive
nodes.body:
• Bone > air conduction
  • WEBER: sound loudest in affected ear
  • RINNE: BC > AC (gap b/w lines in audiogram)
  • DDx: impacted cerumen, foreign body, exostosis, bacterial/fungal/chronic otitis externa, OTITIS MEDIA (→ effusion, adhesive), TM perforations, otosclerosis (mixed hearing loss), temporal bone trauma → ossicular discontinuity
  • Tx: HEARING AIDS, or bone conduction aid ± Sx

nodes.title: Sensorineural
nodes.body:
• Air > bone conduction but ↓↓ overall
  • WEBER: sound loudest in normal ear
  • RINNE: AC > BC (no gap, but overall ↓ in audiogram)
  • DDx: PRESBYCUSIS, congenital, SUDDEN SNHL (emergency), temporal bone trauma, noise-induced, ototoxicity ex. gentamicin, acoustic neuroma (usually UNILATERAL; order MRI for slowly progressive unilateral hearing loss)
  • Tx: COCHLEAR IMPLANTS

nodes.title: Utricle & Saccule (Otolith Organs)
nodes.body:
• "Posture/BALANCE control" (+ cerebellum)
  • Lesions cause VESTIBULAR ATAXIA (+ve Romberg test; see approach to ataxia below)

nodes.title: Semicircular Canals
nodes.body:
• "Image stabilization" on retina/eyes via VOR (+ cerebellum)
  • Lesions cause NYSTAGMUS + VERTIGO

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Nystagmus & Vertigo
nodes.body:
• VERTIGO: illusion of ROTARY movement, often described by pt. as "DIZZINESS"
    • ∴ differentiate from dizziness felt as "lightheaded, unsteady, disoriented", more likely due to cardiac or psychiatric Dx (see calgaryblackbook.ca for DDx)
  • ⭐ NYSTAGMUS: rapid, INVOLUNTARY, small rhythmic eye movements
    • Described according to direction of fast phase (step 6)
    • Need to be conscious (for step 5) to have nystagmus

nodes.title: Central Nystagmus: Brainstem & Cerebellum Dx
nodes.body:
• Lesions of CN VIII, III, IV, VI nuclei, or cerebellar tracts in the brainstem or the cerebellum itself
  • PEx: BILATERAL or unidirectional nystagmus, often w. NEUROLOGIC S/S (brainstem + cerebellar s/s) but rarely auditory s/s; often w. ATAXIA
  • Nystagmus classified as GAZE-EVOKED, rebound, fixed, dissociated…
  • Etiology: see etiologies of cerebellum + brainstem/CNS lesions, ex. MS, basilar A. strokes, tumors, alcohol, Wernicke-Korsakoff, AEDs

nodes.title: Peripheral Nystagmus: Vestibular Apparatus Dx
nodes.body:
• Lesions of the semicircular canals or vestibular fibres in CN VIII
  • PEx: UNIDIRECTIONAL nystagmus, often w. AUDITORY S/S but NO neurologic s/s; often w. N/V
  • Nystagmus classified as SPONTANEOUS (usually horizontal, ↓ w. gaze fixation) or POSITIONAL

nodes.title: Etiologies of Vestibular Dx
nodes.body:
• ❗ BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo): SUDDEN onset vertigo without hearing loss; BRIEF episodes ↑ w. SPECIFIC HEAD MOVEMENTS
    • Caused by trauma → free-floating endolymph particles, often in posterior canal
    • PEx w. +ve response to HALLPIKE maneuver
    • Tx w. EPLEY / Semont maneuver (particle repositioning)
    • Most common Dx
  • SSCD (superior semicircular canal dehiscence): SUDDEN onset vertigo ± hearing loss, ↑ by LOUD & BONE-CONDUCTED SOUNDS
  • MENIERE'S DISEASE: onset over mins-hrs, w. fluctuating HEARING LOSS + TINNITUS
    • Idiopathic ("disease") or 2° to syphilis, trauma or labyrinthitis ("syndrome")
    • → ↑ ENDOLYMPH production or ↓ resorption; ± hydrops
    • Tx w. lifestyle (↓Na+), Rx (diuretics) or ablation Sx
  • VESTIBULAR NEURONITIS: onset over hrs-days; often RECENT URTI; inflammation of vestibular fibres of CN VIII
    • If cochlear fibres also involved: "VIRAL LABYRINTHITIS", also hearing loss + tinnitus
    • Tx w. antiemetics, vestibular sedatives ± steroids
  • GENTAMICIN (aminoglycoside) OTOTOXICITY: unilateral if drops, systemic if p.o.; often permanent s/s

nodes.title: Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR), Cerebellum & Nystagmus
nodes.body: • Title node for the numbered VOR loop (steps 1 to 6), below

nodes.title: Physiologic Nystagmus
nodes.body: • Can be rotatory-induced, caloric-induced ("COWS"), optokinetic & end-point EOM

nodes.title: (1) Semicircular Canals (VOR input)
nodes.body:
• Unequal signal b/w ears indicates head rotation towards side w. ↑↑ signal → VOR INPUT
  • ex. RIGHT head turn detected due to:
    • right-side lesion with ↑↑ signal (ex. BPPV), or
    • left-side lesion with ↓↓ signal (ex. CN VIII neuronitis)

nodes.title: Connections to Vagus Nerve
nodes.body: • Vestibular Dx may have N/V, sweating, ↑ bowel mov.

nodes.title: Reflexes in Legs, Trunk, Arms
nodes.body: • Body tends to FALL to side of vestibular loss

nodes.title: Stimulates the VOR Based on Visual Input
nodes.body:
• Stimulates the VOR based on VISUAL INPUT (retinal slip)
  • + Maintains ECCENTRIC GAZE

nodes.title: (2) Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex Output
nodes.body: • SLOW phase of NYSTAGMUS

nodes.title: (3) VOR → Slow Eye Movement
nodes.body: • VOR → SLOW eye movement in the OPPOSITE direction to head movement (ex. eyes move LEFT)

nodes.title: (4) False/Abnormal Vestibular Signal
nodes.body: • With a false/abnormal vestibular signal (ex. due to BPPV) this drifts gaze away from target

nodes.title: Vertigo
nodes.body: • "Room looks like it's spinning"

nodes.title: (5) Optic Nerve
nodes.body: • Detects visual input from target "drifting off gaze"

nodes.title: Frontal Lobe (Frontal Eye Field), Superior Colliculus, Cerebellum…
(6) Saccades
nodes.body:
• SACCADES = FAST phase of NYSTAGMUS
  • Resets position of the eye to stay on target
  • In this example, moves eyes FAST back to RIGHT, i.e. "RIGHT-BEATING NYSTAGMUS"

nodes.title: Cerebellum 📍
nodes.body: • Controls motor "LEARNING" & COORDINATION of VOLUNTARY motor movements

nodes.title: Etiology of Cerebellar Lesions
nodes.body:
• WERNICKE-KORSAKOFF SYNDROME (THIAMINE/VIT B1 deficiency): 2° to alcohol use, GI malabsorption ex. gastric bypass, IBD…
  • ALCOHOL TOXICITY (cerebellar atrophy or alcohol polyneuropathy)
  • Hereditary ataxias: Friedreich's ataxia, ataxia telangiectasia
  • Other acquired causes: TUMOR, STROKE, hemorrhage, MS, hypothyroidism, toxins (heavy metals, lithium, anticonvulsants)

nodes.title: Functional Subdivisions (of Cerebellum)
nodes.body:
• CEREBRO-CEREBELLUM (in lateral cerebellum)
  • VESTIBULO-CEREBELLUM (in flocculonodular lobe): vestibulo-ocular reflex / VOR; lesions cause NYSTAGMUS…
  • SPINO-CEREBELLUM (in vermis / interm. cerebellum, various sensory inputs): lesions cause HYPOTONIA, TRUNCAL ataxia…

nodes.title: Deficits Due to Lateral Cerebellum (4) Lesions Present IPSILATERALLY Due to This Loop
nodes.body:
• Lesions in steps 1-3, 5-6 present w. contralateral deficits
  • Loop diagram (left hemisphere of brain | midline | RIGHT hemisphere of cerebellum):
    • 1: Motor cortex → internal capsule
    • 2: internal capsule → pons
    • 3: pons → middle cerebellar peduncle → (crosses midline) → cerebellum
    • 4: cerebellum → (crosses back) → thalamus
    • 5: thalamus → motor cortex
    • 6: motor cortex → motor output to RIGHT hemibody via corticospinal tract

nodes.title: Cerebellar Lesions Signs & Symptoms
nodes.body:
• S/S of lesions reflect lack of coordination of the various voluntary muscle regions
  • S/S are IPSILATERAL to lesion ❗
  • Purely cerebellar lesions do NOT cause weakness, hyperreflexia or sensory deficits (not typical UMN s/s)
  • Bracketed s/s list (tile r4c5):
    • Eyes (extraocular muscles via VOR): NYSTAGMUS (yellow dashed "Ataxia of the eyes" → Central Nystagmus)
    • Pharynx (oropharyngeal phase of swallowing): DYSPHAGIA
    • Larynx (speech): DYSARTHRIA (→ Cerebellar (Ataxic) Dysarthria)
    • Limbs (gait, hand dexterity):
      • DYSDIADOCHOKINESIA (difficulty w. rapid alternating movements)
      • INTENTION TREMOR (but no resting tremor)
      • ATAXIA: DYSMETRIA (failed finger-to-nose (FTN), heel-to-shin (HTS) tests)
      • ATAXIC GAIT (wide stance, drunk-like, and tandem gait impairment (heel-toe walk))
    • ↓ → Cerebellar Ataxia

nodes.title: Cerebellar (Ataxic) Dysarthria
nodes.body:
• aka "SCANNING" dysarthria (irregular rhythm & pitch)
  • Spinal-cerebellar ataxia
  • MS, alcohol, tumor

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Dysarthria
nodes.body:
• Difficulties w. articulation, aka SLURRED SPEECH
  • Shared CN IX and CN X innervation of phonation (larynx) + swallowing (pharynx), plus proximity of CN nuclei/nerves in medulla/jugular foramen → dysarthria often presents w. DYSPHAGIA (difficulty swallowing)
  • Main Invx for oropharyngeal dysphagia: MODIFIED BARIUM SWALLOW ❗
  • Main Invx for esophageal dysphagia:
    • If mechanical Dx (solids only): ENDOSCOPY
    • If motility Dx (solids + liquids): MANOMETRY
  • (Review PoM II Otolaryngology)

nodes.title: LMN Dysarthria
nodes.body:
• Slow, low volume, breathy speech
  • CN IX, X, XII LESIONS, including CN nuclei w. BRAINSTEM/MEDULLA LESION ❗
  • Myasthenia gravis
  • Muscular dystrophy
  • Neuropathy (recurrent laryngeal N. lesion)

nodes.title: UMN Dysarthria
nodes.body:
• Slow, strangulated, harsh voice
  • Cortical lesion (in mouth area of homunculus, MCA region), MS, ALS

nodes.title: Extra-Pyramidal (Dysarthria)
nodes.body:
• Rapid, low volume, monotone speech
  • Parkinson's disease

nodes.title: Cerebellar Ataxia
nodes.body: • Pt presents w. other s/s of cerebellar lesions (see above)

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Ataxia
nodes.body:
• Difficulty w. coordination in movements/muscles, aka UNSTEADINESS
  • May lead to FALLS ❗
  • 3 main tracts (in addition to cerebellum) contribute to motor coordination/balance:
    • Vestibular
    • Proprioception
    • Visual
  • Posture can be maintained (i.e. not falling over) if 2/3 of these are functioning; can be used to narrow down DDx for ataxia via Romberg test

nodes.title: Romberg Test
nodes.body: • Ask pt to close eyes: visual tract removed, leaving the minimum 2/3 tracts required to maintain posture

nodes.title: Positive Romberg Sign
nodes.body:
• Unsteadiness worsens or failure to maintain posture (i.e. patient falls) w. eyes closed
  • ∴ Vestibular or proprioception tracts are abnormal

nodes.title: Negative Romberg Sign
nodes.body:
• Minimal changes to unsteadiness (compared to when eyes were open)
  • ∴ Vestibular + proprioception tracts are normal

nodes.title: Vestibular Ataxia
nodes.body:
• Pt often presents w. ataxia AND VERTIGO + NYSTAGMUS
  • ± Hearing deficit
  • (See vestibular lesions above)

nodes.title: Peripheral Nerve
nodes.body:
• Sensory loss due to peripheral nerve (peripheral sensory nerve lesion)
  • ↓ Proprioception via large fibers
  • Pt often presents w. ataxia AND other s/s of peripheral nerve lesion, i.e. paresthesias, numbness
  • Look for RFs: DM, chemotherapy

nodes.title: Other Causes of Unsteadiness/Ataxia
nodes.body:
• Muscle WEAKNESS
  • Systemic Dx (CVD, infections…)
  • VISUAL ATAXIA

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Gait Disturbance
nodes.body:
• 3 main components of gait control (central motor systems):
    • CEREBELLUM: affects coordination of movements for gait → ATAXIC GAIT: wide-based gait, "DRUNK-LIKE" unsteadiness
    • PYRAMIDAL: main motor outflow from cortex to spinal cord → SPASTIC GAIT: spastic (stiff) foot drop, toe walking, circumduction, scissoring (cortex lesion: unilateral; cord lesion: bilateral)
    • BASAL GANGLIA (extrapyramidal): basal ganglia inhibits excess movements
      • PARKINSONIAN gait: small steps, reduced armswing
      • Choreic / hemiballistic / dystonic gait
  • VS Gait disturbance by muscle WEAKNESS or pain:
    • STEPPAGE gait: due to FOOT DROP from LMN lesion (ex. peroneal N. lesion, L5 radiculopathy)
    • ANTALGIC gait: due to MSK pain (pt avoids putting weight on affected limb)
    • OR other gait types, ex. Trendelenburg gait…

nodes.title: Intention Tremor
nodes.body:
• Test via FINGER TO NOSE (FTN) or HEEL TO SHIN (HTS) PEx
  • Etiology: CEREBELLAR pathology, Wilson's disease, MS, alcohol (delirium tremens)…

nodes.title: Postural Tremor
nodes.body: • Test via SUSTAINED POSTURE, ex. outstretched hands

nodes.title: Essential Tremor
nodes.body:
• Etiology: CEREBELLAR + pons Dx ± hereditary
  • PEx: SYMMETRIC, affects arms, HEAD (head titubation / "yes-yes") + voice
  • Tremor worse w. ACTION or sustained posture; LARGE HANDWRITING + tremulous; worsens w. time
  • Tremor IMPROVES w. ALCOHOL ❗
  • Tx: do not Tx if mild; responds to BETA BLOCKERS or anticonvulsants; if refractory: DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION

nodes.title: Other Causes of Postural Tremor
nodes.body:
• Enhanced PHYSIOLOGIC tremor
  • Metabolic (HYPERTHYROIDISM, liver or kidney dx, ↑BG…)
  • DRUG-INDUCED TREMOR: salbutamol or PREDNISONE ❗

nodes.title: Action Tremors
nodes.body: • Tremor worse with ACTION + PEx WITHOUT TRAP symptoms

nodes.title: Resting Tremor (TRAP)
nodes.body: • Tremor worse at REST + PEx with TRAP symptoms

nodes.title: Basal Ganglia: Movement Disorders 📍
nodes.body:
• Basal ganglia consists of five deep grey matter regions:
    • Caudate nucleus (red dot) + Putamen (purple dot) = STRIATUM (ventral striatum = nucleus accumbens); internal capsule (dotted line) between caudate and putamen
    • Putamen + Globus pallidus (blue dot) = Lentiform nucleus
    • Subthalamic nucleus
    • Substantia nigra
  • Brain images: coronal section and sagittal 3D view with coloured dots matching the key (red caudate, purple putamen, blue globus pallidus, green thalamus; other grey/brown dots unlabelled)
  • Cortical input and output regulated by the THALAMUS (green dot); thalamus under chronic INHIBITION by the basal ganglia
  • → Basal ganglia "RELEASES THE INHIBITION" of appropriate movements (direct pathway) and suppresses inappropriate movements (indirect pathway) → RELEASE INHIBITION MODEL

nodes.title: Release Inhibition Model / Direct Pathway (↑ Cortex Output)
nodes.body:
• Diagram: Substantia nigra →(+)1 Caudate & putamen; Cortex →(+) Caudate & putamen; Caudate/putamen →(−)2 Globus pallidus int.; GPi →(−, chronic) Thalamus; Thalamus --(+)3--> Cortex
  • 1. Excitatory signal from subs. nigra via DOPAMINE
  • 2. Inhibits the chronic inhibition to the thalamus
  • 3. ↑ Excitation of cortex, ↑ CORTICAL MOTOR OUTPUT
  • Substantia nigra lesions associated w. PARKINSON'S DISEASE
  • (Indirect pathway: step 2 is (+) ∴ ↑ inhibition of thalamus and ↓ cortical output; lesions here associated w. HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE)

nodes.title: Basal Ganglia Controls Initiation & Timing
nodes.body:
• Basal ganglia controls INITIATION & TIMING of voluntary motor movements
  • Do NOT control balance/motor coordination ⭐
  • Lesions can result in hypo- or hyper-kinetic disorders

nodes.title: Hypokinetic Disorders aka Parkinsonism
nodes.body:
• Clinical syndrome w. typical "TRAP" symptoms:
    • T: TREMOR (resting), often "pill rolling" tremor, ASYMMETRIC
    • R: RIGIDITY (velocity independent HYPERTONIA)
    • A: AKINESIA (difficult to initiate moves) + BRADYKINESIA (slow)
    • P: POSTURAL INSTABILITY (takes >2 steps or falls w. TUG test)
  • Tremor + Rigidity = "COG WHEEL RIGIDITY"
  • Etiologies: PD (most common), PSP, MSA, others

nodes.title: Other Causes of Parkinsonism
nodes.body:
• Basal ganglia pathology (stroke, bleeds, tumors…)
  • Repeated head trauma
  • Lewy body disease
  • Toxins (ex. carbon monoxide, cyanide)
  • DRUG-INDUCED PARKINSONISM: antipsychotics + antiemetics ex. Stemetil + METOCLOPRAMIDE ❗ (D2 receptor antagonist, Tx of gastroparesis)

nodes.title: Multiple Systems Atrophy (MSA)
nodes.body:
• Neurodegenerative Dx + AUTONOMIC nervous system dysfunction + one of: parkinsonism (MSA-P) or cerebellar dysfunction (MSA-C)
  • Prognosis: worse than PD; death within 6-9 yrs of onset

nodes.title: Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP)
nodes.body:
• PEx: parkinsonism/TRAPs but axial tone > limb tone ∴ "STIFF NECK" + ↓ balance
  • + VERTICAL SUPRANUCLEAR GAZE PALSY: impaired voluntary VERTICAL GAZE movements, but moving the head (vestibular input) gives normal vertical eye movements
  • Tx: does NOT respond to L-DOPA
  • Prognosis: worse than PD; survival 4-7 yrs after onset

nodes.title: Parkinson's Disease
nodes.body:
• Pathophys: familial or sporadic (most common) degeneration of DOPAMINE-producing neurons in SUBSTANTIA NIGRA
  • PEx: ASYMMETRIC + BILATERAL parkinsonism/TRAP, hypomimia / ↓ facial expression + ↓ blinking, hypophonia, stooped posture, ↓ arm swing w. gait, turning "en bloc", SMALL HANDWRITING…
  • Diagnosis: CLINICAL Dx; no Invx necessary if typical s/s + no other cause of s/s (ex. meds, stroke…)
  • Tx: treat when bradykinesia + rigidity LIMIT FUNCTION; do NOT treat if asymptomatic or if TREMOR is the only s/s (Tx resistant)
    • Dopamine replacement with LEVODOPA (crosses BBB); cannot be stopped suddenly (continue Tx even if NPO)
    • Early Dx may be Tx w. MAO-B inhibitors, dopamine agonists + anticholinergics for prominent tremors
  • Prognosis: PROGRESSIVE worsening w. time, dyskinesias w. Tx, depression + dementia; death usually due to aspiration pneumonia

nodes.title: Complications of Chronic L-Dopa
nodes.body:
• 50% of pts treated >5 yrs
  • DYSKINESIAS: abnormal, involuntary moves, ex. CHOREA or DYSTONIA
  • When med dose wears off: dyskinesia/"on" → akinesia/"off" (i.e. motor fluctuations)

nodes.title: Hyperkinetic Disorders
nodes.body:
• PEx: hemiballismus (kicks), chorea (dance-like), tics, athetosis (slow dance), tremors, dystonia (fixed posture), myoclonus
  • Each presentation has a different set of etiologies/DDx

nodes.title: Hemiballismus
nodes.body:
• Rapid irregular movements on side of body contralateral to basal ganglia lesion (often vascular)
  • ex. acute onset due to stroke

nodes.title: Chorea
nodes.body: • (Covered in OSSO [?])

nodes.title: Levodopa-Induced Dyskinesia
nodes.body:
• Most common cause of chorea
  • (or other meds/drugs, ex. anti-psychotics, cocaine)
  • PD treated w. chronic L-dopa resembles Huntington's Dx

nodes.title: Huntington's Disease
nodes.body:
• Pathophys: triple nucleotide repeat Dx w. ANTICIPATION (↑ size of repeat w. each generation → earlier onset + more severe Dx)
  • Autosomal DOMINANT ∴ 50% risk of offspring inheritance
  • HTT gene encodes C-A-G repeats; if >40 repeats (full penetrance) → accumulation of defective proteins in neurons → degeneration of neurons → global CEREBRAL ATROPHY, especially in CAUDATE NUCLEUS → ↑ activity of direct pathway, ↓ activity of indirect pathway
  • PEx: PSYCHIATRIC s/s and neurologic s/s (CHOREA → dystonia, rigidity; memory and intellectual impairments)
    • Age of onset approx. 40 y.o. (varies w. anticipation)
    • Progression of s/s to death in 15-25 yrs
  • Invx: GENETIC TESTING (± pre-symptomatic test for relatives) + MRI (atrophy of cortex + caudate nucleus)
  • Tx: no cure; supportive only

nodes.title: Sydenham Chorea
nodes.body:
• Post-strep infection, in acute rheumatic fever
  • Hx of recent Group A strep pharyngitis
  • Invx w. ASO (anti-streptolysin O titer)

nodes.title: Other Causes of Chorea
nodes.body:
• Basal ganglia infarction, tumor: Invx w. MRI (assess basal ganglia)
  • Hyperthyroidism: Invx w. metabolic workup
  • Pregnancy (chorea gravidarum)

nodes.title: Primary Headaches
nodes.body: • Usually episodic; must RULE OUT 2° headaches in Hx/PEx, look for red flags

nodes.title: Cluster Headache
nodes.body:
• aka "SUICIDE" headache
  • UNILATERAL, often peri-ORBITAL (CN V1 region); severe pain, "sharp" headache
  • Other s/s: ipsilateral AUTONOMIC s/s (nasal congestion, LACRIMATION, rhinorrhea, miosis) + sense of RESTLESSNESS or agitation (often walking around...)
  • Duration: <3 hrs, fast onset, MULTIPLE attacks/day, REPEAT in similar "clusters" of time daily
  • Associations: men, SMOKING
  • Invx: must order brain MRI ❗ to rule out compressive lesions
  • Tx: oxygen (100% FiO2), SUMATRIPTAN (SC)

nodes.title: Tension Headache
nodes.body:
• MOST COMMON headaches
  • BILATERAL "band-like", mild-moderate pain, "pressing, tight, dull" headaches
  • Other s/s: may have MSK PERICRANIAL TENDERNESS; no worsening w. activity; no neurologic s/s
  • + NO N/V ❗; no more than ONE of phono- or photophobia
  • Duration: variable, 30 mins to 7 days
  • Tx: NSAIDs, acetaminophen and/or conservative

nodes.title: Migraines
nodes.body:
• With or without AURA
  • UNILATERAL, moderate to severe pain, "throbbing or PULSATING" headache
  • Other s/s: ≥1 of NAUSEA and/or VOMITING, or phonophobia and PHOTOPHOBIA; may worsen w. activity / are DISABLING (often in dark rooms resting...)
  • ± AURA: reversible neurological symptoms that precede or accompany migraine headache (<1 hr)
    • usually VISUAL (ex. scintillating scotomas, vision loss) ± sensory (ex. numbness, tingling), speech and/or language problems; less commonly motor + brainstem deficits
    • may mimic STROKE s/s ❗
  • Duration: 4-72 HOURS
  • Associations: women, genetic predisposition, STRESS...

nodes.title: Management of Migraines
nodes.body:
• Migraine pathophys: abnormal activation of trigeminal afferent fibers → ↑CGRP (vasoactive peptides) → VASODILATION of intracranial vessels → plasma protein extravasation w. INFLAMMATORY mediators → pain
  • ∴ one goal of Tx is to ↑VASOCONSTRICTION
  • Acute Tx
    • 1st line SUMATRIPTAN (5-HT1B/1D serotonin receptor agonist → ↓CGRP) ± NSAIDs ± anti-emetics (ex. metoclopramide)
    • Triptans ↑BP ∴ don't combine w. other drugs that ↑BP; contraindicated for pt. w. CAD, CVD, HTN, stroke, pregnancy...
    • Triptans ↑serotonin receptors ∴ risk of serotonin syndrome if combined w. SSRIs
    • Treat EARLY in attack; <2-3 days/week to ↓medication-overuse headache
  • Preventative Tx
    • PROPRANOLOL or metoprolol (anti-HTN BETA-BLOCKERS): CI if asthma, DM
    • AMITRIPTYLINE (anti-depressant): ↑weight
    • TOPIRAMATE (anti-epileptic): ↓weight
    • ONABOTULINUMTOXIN A: approved for chronic migraines only
    • Supplements ex. Mg, B2, Q10
    • CGRP monoclonal antibodies

nodes.title: Secondary Headaches
nodes.body: • Usually constant, w. associated RED FLAG s/s listed below

nodes.title: Other 2° Headaches
nodes.body: • Without red flag s/s: sinusitis, dental abscess, CONCUSSION, dehydration, substance withdrawal, medication overuse

nodes.title: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension
nodes.body:
• Young, obese females; excess vitamin A → ↑ICP; normal ventricle size → non-localized ↑ICP HEADACHES
  • LP → ↑opening pressure; diagnostic + therapeutic

nodes.title: Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension
nodes.body:
• CSF leakage due to tear in arachnoid → ↓CSF pressure → ↓ICP POSTURAL HEADACHE: improves w. supine
  • Opposite s/s to ↑ICP headache
  • (Covered in DSSG)

nodes.title: GCA Headache
nodes.body:
• S/S: new TEMPLE headache in pt. >50 y.o. (review Rheum)
  • Invx: labs w. CRP, ESR; temporal A. biopsy
  • Start Tx ASAP, risk of VISION LOSS
  • (Review GCA in Rheum map)

nodes.title: Meningitis Headache
nodes.body:
• S/S: w. FEVER + chills, NECK STIFFNESS, Brudzinski or Kernig sign ± photophobia...
  • ↑risk if IMMUNOSUPPRESSION...
  • Invx: labs (CBC), CT/MRI, LP CSF

nodes.title: SAH Headache
nodes.body:
• S/S: SUDDEN onset of worst headache / THUNDERCLAP
  • Invx: non-contrast CT

nodes.title: ↑ICP Headache (Tumor, Hematoma...)
nodes.body:
• S/S: headache worse when SUPINE, in MORNINGS, ± N/V, altered LOC (↓GCS), PAPILLEDEMA, other FOCAL neurological s/s
  • Invx: non-contrast CT for bleed, w. contrast for tumor
  • (Review ICP headaches segment below)

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Acute + Transient Loss of Consciousness
nodes.body: • (vs. acute and ONGOING LOC would have different DDx ex. strokes...)

nodes.title: Metabolic (LOC)
nodes.body:
• ex. hypoglycemia
  • Invx: BG, lytes, TSH...

nodes.title: Less Common Causes (LOC)
nodes.body: • Pseudoseizures (psychogenic event), sleep disorder, BRAINSTEM TIA (affecting RAS), transient ↑ICP (hydrocephalus, very rare)

nodes.title: Syncope
nodes.body:
• Insufficient cerebral perfusion
  • REFLEX syncope: VASOVAGAL episode or other cause of HYPOTENSION
  • CARDIAC syncope: ARRHYTHMIA, cardiac outflow obstruction...
  • Invx w. ECG ± labs (CK, troponin, BNP), echo, CXR

nodes.title: Seizures (LOC branch)
nodes.body:
• If unwitnessed seizure, post-ictal period may mimic other Dx ex. stroke
  • Invx: EEG + CT/MRI...

nodes.title: Transient Focal Neurologic S/S
nodes.body: • Can be caused by TIAs, seizure post-ictal s/s and migraine auras (usually visual s/s, <1 hr)

nodes.title: Post-Ictal Syndromes
nodes.body:
• S/S during period of time AFTER a seizure, usually where the seizure was w. IMPAIRED AWARENESS:
    • confusion, aphasia, fatigue
    • weakness aka TODD'S PARESIS ⭐ (REVERSIBLE and TRANSIENT)
  • Persistent focal deficits should prompt urgent Invx

nodes.title: Status Epilepticus
nodes.body:
• Single seizure ≥5 MINUTES, or multiple seizures w. incomplete LOC regained b/w each episode
  • Medical EMERGENCY: can cause irreversible brain damage w/o Tx
  • Tx: abort seizure w. IV BENZODIAZEPINES (lorazepam/Ativan); prevent recurrence w. IV PHENYTOIN (Dilantin)

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Seizures
nodes.body:
• Definition: transient s/s due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity
  • Clinical presentation
    • MOTOR (CONVULSIVE): tonic ("stiff") and/or clonic ("rhythmic") contractions, myoclonic (non-rhythmic jerking movements), automatisms (ex. lip smacking), atonic...
    • NON-MOTOR: SENSORY disturbances (numbness, auditory or visual hallucinations...), cognitive, BEHAVIOURAL, altered consciousness (ex. "blank stare"...), urinary incontinence...
    • PEx after seizure: TONGUE bites, MSK injuries, post-ictal s/s; often NORMAL

nodes.title: Acute Management of First Seizure
nodes.body:
• PEx for additional s/s indicative of meningitis, stroke or ↑ICP that could be causing seizure → CT ± LP
  • Invx for 2° causes: CBC, lytes, Ca2+, glucose, Cr, LFTs, CK, toxicology, EtOH → if +ve: CT + outpatient EEG
  • If no 2° cause identified → EPILEPSY PROTOCOL: assess for CNS lesions + temporal lobes via MRI SCAN ❗ and ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY (EEG); note EEG is specific but not sensitive; ± CT done in ER
    • First episode of single unprovoked seizure w. no CT/MRI/EEG findings: do NOT treat w. AEDs
  • By Canadian law, MTO must be contacted for all pts w. a seizure; pt will have license suspended until seizure-free for 6 months; commercial drivers may face a longer wait

nodes.title: Classification of Seizures
nodes.body: • Further subclassified according to s/s (see clin. presentation)

nodes.title: Focal Seizures
nodes.body:
• ↑activity in ONE hemisphere region → CONTRALATERAL s/s (motor or non-motor)
  • ± AURA/"warning"; old name: PARTIAL seizures
  • Subtypes: focal AWARE (simple partial) or focal IMPAIRED AWARENESS (complex partial)

nodes.title: Generalized Seizures
nodes.body:
• ↑activity in BOTH hemispheres → BILATERAL s/s, usually MOTOR s/s (non-motor s/s in absence subtype)
  • Almost always w. IMPAIRED AWARENESS ∴ w. POST-ICTAL s/s (no post-ictal in absences)
  • Subtypes: ABSENCE seizures, generalized TONIC-CLONIC (grand mal)...
  • If unwitnessed onset: "UNKNOWN onset" classification

nodes.title: Etiology of Seizures
nodes.body: • TRIGGERS such as flashing lights, fevers (in children), ↓sleep, alcohol, dehydration... ↓seizure threshold and can cause REFLEX seizures

nodes.title: Primary (Seizures)
nodes.body: • Unprovoked / epileptic

nodes.title: Epilepsy
nodes.body:
• Definition: enduring PREDISPOSITION to generate epileptic seizures
  • Etiology: old CNS lesions (*): prior STROKES (#1 cause of late-onset seizures in pt >50 y.o.), MESIAL TEMPORAL SCLEROSIS (#1 cause in adults <50 y.o.), tumor, genetic, prior infections: NEUROCYSTICERCOSIS (#1 cause worldwide), autoimmune (ex. anti-NMDA-r Ab), PERINATAL insult, congenital
  • Diagnostic criteria: ≥2 unprovoked (or reflex) seizures >24 hrs apart, OR Dx of epilepsy syndrome, OR 1 unprovoked (or reflex) seizure AND >60% risk of recurrence (ex. evidence of stroke, tumor or other lesion on CT/MRI)
  • Risk factors: Hx of childhood/febrile seizures, Hx of head trauma or CNS infections, FHx of seizures/epilepsy
  • Chronic Tx: ANTIEPILEPTIC DRUGS (AEDs): PHENYTOIN, VALPROATE, levetiracetam ("KEPPRA"), benzodiazepines...
    • ⇢ various considerations when choosing AEDs: side effects, interactions, TERATOGENIC AEDs...
  • Tx of drug-resistant epilepsy: failure of 2 AEDs → refer to EPILEPSY CENTER → alt. Tx such as responsive neurostimulation (RNS), vagus N. stimulation, intracranial monitoring + resection surgery (ex. mesial temporal lobe)

nodes.title: Hydrocephalus
nodes.body: • ↑CSF production or ↓CSF drainage → enlarged ventricles

nodes.title: Hydrocephalus Ex-Vacuo
nodes.body: • Dementia (AD), AIDS, Huntington's Dx → diffuse CORTICAL ATROPHY → normal ICP and ventriculomegaly proportional to cortical atrophy

nodes.title: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus
nodes.body:
• Same etiology as communicating type → ↓resorption of CSF AND some cortical atrophy → normal ICP and ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy
  • Classic PEx TRIAD "wobbly, wet + wonky": GAIT ATAXIA, URINARY INCONTINENCE, DEMENTIA ❗
  • Symptomatic improvement w. high-volume LUMBAR PUNCTURE and/or VP SHUNT

nodes.title: Communicating Hydrocephalus
nodes.body:
• Subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis → scarring of arachnoid granulations → ↓resorption of CSF ("communicating" bc. no obstruction b/w ventricles) → ↑ICP and ventriculomegaly to all ventricular system (diffuse)
  • Also caused by choroid plexus papilloma → ↑CSF production

nodes.title: Non-Communicating (Obstructive) Hydrocephalus
nodes.body:
• ICH, MENINGITIS, malformations → scarring or mass lesions along CSF path/ventricles (ex. at cerebral aqueduct) → ↓CSF drainage/flow → ↑ICP and ventriculomegaly proximal to obstruction → if untreated: ↑ICP causes HERNIATION
  • Tx: acutely w. external ventricular drain; if chronic w. VP SHUNT (ventricles → peritoneum) to drain CSF

nodes.title: Brain Tumors
nodes.body:
• PEx: PERSISTENT + POSITIONAL (↑ICP) HEADACHE (ex. worse w. supine, coughing...) w. N/V; FOCAL s/s ex. weakness, sensory, gait; change in cognition; SEIZURES (often focal)
  • Key red flag: s/s progression over WEEKS-MONTHS, or longer if slow-growing
  • Diagnosis via IMAGING: gadolinium CONTRAST-ENHANCED MRI SCAN ❗
    • If CT scan is used it must be contrast enhanced; contrast highlights BBB breakdown (enhancement often = high grade)
    • Confirm Dx via tissue resection or biopsy
  • Tx: ↓headaches w. STEROIDS (edema), anti-epileptic if seizures, Sx + radiation

nodes.title: 1° CNS Lymphoma
nodes.body:
• Primary brain tumor
  • Immunosuppressed, ↑age, HIV higher risk
  • B-CELL NON-HODGKIN lymphoma restricted to CNS (i.e. not a metastasis of systemic lymphoma)

nodes.title: Brain Metastases
nodes.body:
• Secondary brain tumor; MOST COMMON CNS tumors
  • 1° sources: most common LUNG (small cell, adenocarcinoma), breast, melanoma, renal cell; other rare types ex. prostate, GI...
  • MRI: MULTIPLE mets, highly ENHANCING lesions ± necrotic core → follow-up w. CHEST X-RAY for 1° lung tumor...
  • Tx: if deep lesion: biopsy; if safe/accessible: RESECTION → RADIATION

nodes.title: Paraneoplastic Neurologic Syndromes
nodes.body:
• Most are IMMUNE (antibody) mediated; examples:
    • small cell lung cancer → Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar Dx, limbic encephalitis...
    • thymoma → myasthenia gravis
  • Cancer Tx can also cause neurological Dx:
    • chemotherapy → peripheral neuropathy
    • immunotherapy ex. immune checkpoint inhibitors → AUTOIMMUNE Dx: myositis, myasthenia gravis...

nodes.title: Gliomas
nodes.body:
• Most common type of PRIMARY brain tumors
  • Grade I gliomas (pilocytic astrocytoma) are benign; grade III-IV are malignant; ASTROCYTOMA subtypes more aggressive
  • IDH mutation + 1p/19q co-deletion: molecular biomarkers w. better prognosis

nodes.title: Low Grade Glioma
nodes.body:
• Malignant grade II glioma
  • MRI: NON-ENHANCING hypointense area
  • Tx: if seizures only or asymptomatic: anti-epileptics + serial MRIs; if symptomatic/worsening MRI/pt preference: confirm Dx w. BIOPSY or RESECTION if accessible → RADIATION Tx ± chemo, for some
  • Prognosis: 5-15 yrs median survival

nodes.title: Anaplastic Oligodendroglioma
nodes.body:
• Malignant grade III / anaplastic glioma
  • MRI: heterogenous, slightly ENHANCING core

nodes.title: Glioblastoma Multiforme
nodes.body:
• Malignant grade IV glioma
  • MRI: highly ENHANCING, central NECROTIC CORE, may cross midline (corpus callosum) ant. or post., BUTTERFLY-shaped
  • Tx: if deep lesion: STEREOTACTIC BIOPSY to confirm Dx; if safe/accessible lesion: maximum Sx RESECTION → chemotherapy + radiation; treat IMMEDIATELY even if no s/s; treat s/s ex. ↓headache w. STEROIDS
  • Prognosis: not curable ∴ very poor; Sx + Rx + chemo = 40% 2-YEAR survival; ↓prognosis if old age or poor neurological function

nodes.title: Hemorrhage
nodes.body: • Classified according to location of bleed: epidural, subdural, subarachnoid or intracerebral

nodes.title: Epidural Hematoma
nodes.body:
• Location: tight potential space b/w dura and skull
  • Common cause: rupture of MIDDLE MENINGEAL A. due to fracture of temporal bone (pterion) by head TRAUMA
  • PEx: brief LOC → LUCID INTERVAL (no s/s for few hrs) → s/s of ↑ICP and HERNIATION (see below: pupil dilation, coma...)
  • Invx: NON-CONTRAST CT scan w. hyperdense (bright) acute blood forming LENS-SHAPED biconvex hematoma (blood doesn't spread across cranial sutures where dura inserts)
  • Tx: emergency CRANIOTOMY if >1 cm or symptomatic; good prognosis if early Tx

nodes.title: Subdural Hematoma
nodes.body:
• Location: loose potential space b/w dura and arachnoid
  • Common cause: rupture of BRIDGING VEINS, vulnerable as they cross from subarachnoid into dural sinuses
  • Invx: non-contrast CT w. blood forming CRESCENT-SHAPED hematoma (blood spreads easily b/w loosely adherent dura + arachnoid)

nodes.title: Chronic Subdural Hematoma
nodes.body:
• Common cause: ELDERLY pt. w. brain ATROPHY → bridging veins more susceptible to shear injuries with or WITHOUT Hx of TRAUMA
  • PEx: venous blood oozes slowly (wks to months) → brain accommodates → VAGUE s/s: headache, cognitive impairment or unsteady gait ± focal s/s
  • Invx: non-contrast CT w. old blood (1-2 wks isodense, 3-4 wks hypodense/dark) and new blood (hyperdense/bright) mixed (HEMATOCRIT EFFECT) in a CRESCENT shape

nodes.title: Acute Subdural Hematoma
nodes.body:
• Common cause: high velocity impact → head ACCELERATION + DECELERATION shearing the bridging veins; impact also causes traumatic SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE and brain CONTUSION (+ diffuse axonal injury)
  • ∴ HIGH MORTALITY (↑ if ↑ICP, >65 y.o., Sx >4 hrs)
  • PEx: LOC at scene, persistent COMA, s/s of ↑ICP and HERNIATION
  • Invx: acute ∴ hyperdense crescent on CT

nodes.title: Hemorrhagic Strokes
nodes.body: • Etiologies labelled by (pink target) symbol

nodes.title: Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH)
nodes.body:
• Location: within brain PARENCHYMA in cortex, brainstem, cerebellum...
  • Common cause: rupture of pial + PENETRATING CEREBRAL VESSELS
  • Invx: non-contrast CT w. hyperdense blood (acute) WITHIN BRAIN TISSUE

nodes.title: Non-Traumatic Intracerebral Hemorrhage
nodes.body:
• Common causes: HYPERTENSION (ex. cocaine, essential HTN...), AMYLOID ANGIOPATHY, arteriovenous malformations, brain tumors, COAGULOPATHY, infections, 2° to PRIOR ISCHEMIC INFARCT, vasculitis...
  • PEx depends on etiology + location of bleed:
    • HYPERTENSIVE ARTERIOPATHY: common sites DEEP: BASAL GANGLIA, thalamus, cerebellum and pons (see Dx in map for s/s) → often affect small vessels: LACUNAR STROKES
    • AMYLOID ANGIOPATHY: LOBAR HEMORRHAGES; SUPERFICIAL, in white matter just under cortex of frontal, parietal, temporal or occipital lobe; tend to be RECURRENT or multiple, in older pts
  • Management of ICH STROKE: BP control, hold all antiplatelets/anticoags, DVT prophylaxis mechanically (LMWH after 24 hrs + stable on CT); Invx cause; OT, PT

nodes.title: Traumatic Intracerebral Hemorrhage
nodes.body:
• Common cause: high velocity impact → head ACCELERATION + DECELERATION shearing of small penetrating vessels: small PETECHIAL HEMORRHAGES + larger confluent INTRAPARENCHYMAL HEMORRHAGE
  • PEx: varies based on severity and co-existing lesions
  • Invx: petechial bleeds difficult to see acutely on CT; intraparenchymal bleeds large + hyperdense on CT

nodes.title: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH)
nodes.body:
• Location: CSF-filled subarachnoid space b/w arachnoid and pia
  • Common cause: rupture of MAJOR CEREBRAL VESSELS (ex. PCommA, MCA...) → blood mixes w. CSF in subarachnoid space
  • PEx: SUDDEN catastrophic headache, "THUNDERCLAP HEADACHE" (pt often describes it as "worst headache of their life" or "head exploding") due to MENINGEAL IRRITATION by blood (meninges highly innervated) → N/V
  • Invx: non-contrast CT scan w. hyperdense blood DIFFUSELY IN SUBARACHNOID space and TRACKS DOWN INTO SULCI following contours of pia

nodes.title: Non-Traumatic (Spontaneous) Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
nodes.body:
• Common cause: rarely bleeds from AVMs and other rare Dx; vast majority due to RUPTURED ANEURYSMS:
    • saccular or berry aneurysms usually arise from arterial BRANCH points/bifurcations near the CIRCLE OF WILLIS, usually from INTERNAL CAROTID: anterior comm. A (most common), post. comm. A and middle cerebral A
    • large unruptured aneurysms can present w. s/s due to mass effects, ex. PComm.A aneurysm → CN III compression (see CN segment of map ⭐)
  • Invx: NON-CONTRAST CT w. hyperdense/bright blood WITHIN SULCI; if ↑suspicion but NEGATIVE CT scan → LP for XANTHOCHROMIA; next Invx: CT ANGIOGRAM to define exact location of aneurysm
  • Tx: Sx placement of clip across neck of aneurysm, or interventional Rx placement of detachable coils within aneurysm
  • Risks of rebleeding and post-SAH VASOSPASM

nodes.title: Traumatic Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
nodes.body:
• Common cause: high velocity impact → head ACCELERATION + DECELERATION → rupture cerebral vessels + CONTUSION + SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE
  • PEx: severe headache + other s/s depending on co-existing lesions

nodes.title: Traumatic Brain Injuries
nodes.body:
• Fractures ex. BASILAR SKULL FRACTURE w. RACCOON EYES + CSF rhinorrhea...
  • Focal injuries ex. CONTUSIONS, hematomas, GSW...
  • Diffuse injuries ex. CONCUSSION, diffuse axonal...
  • Assess Dx severity (3-15) with GLASGOW COMA SCALE (GCS):
    • EYE OPENING (1-4): 1 none, 2 to pain, 3 to speech, 4 spontaneously
    • VERBAL RESPONSE (1-5): 1 none, 2 incomprehensible, 3 inappropriate, 4 confused, 5 oriented
    • MOTOR RESPONSE (1-6): 1 none, 2 extension to pain, 3 flexion to pain, 4 withdraws from pain, 5 localizes pain, 6 obeys commands
    • Reported as E_V_M: ex. E2V3M4 = GCS 9; INTUBATE if GCS ≤8 for airway protection

nodes.title: Acceleration-Deceleration Contusion
nodes.body:
• ex. motor vehicle accidents, falling on ice...
  • CONTUSION at site of impact (COUP-injury) and side opposite to impact (CONTRECOUP) bc. of rebound/inertia of brain against skull (most commonly FRONTAL + TEMPORAL lobe) → damage to underlying nervous tissue (necrosis), axonal tracts + blood vessels (bridging veins, cerebral vessels and small penetrating vessels) → CO-EXISTING LESIONS (labelled by yellow symbol)
  • Invx: in a DELAYED non-contrast CT (24-48 hrs) may see MULTIPLE small hyperdense/bright areas of blood from PETECHIAL HEMORRHAGES surrounded by HYPODENSE/dark areas of NECROSIS and EDEMA

nodes.title: Diffuse Axonal Injury
nodes.body:
• Due to head acceleration-deceleration (ex. MVAs, or SHAKING BABY SYNDROME)
  • Grey-white matter junction (different densities ∴ acceleration/inertia separates them)
  • Structures fixed in relation to rest of brain ∴ more susceptible to injury: corpus callosum, dorsolateral pons, cervicomedullary junction
  • Bleeding from PETECHIAL hemorrhages also ↑injury to white matter tracts

nodes.title: Etiologies of Ischemic Strokes
nodes.body:
• THROMBOSIS (small vessel occlusion/LACUNAR STROKE, or large vessel occlusion ex. MCA) due to ATHEROSCLEROSIS/HTN or arterial dissection (ex. vertebral or carotid A.)
  • EMBOLUS from artery (aorta, carotid A, or intracranial A. STENOSIS) or from HEART/cardioembolic (AFIB, valvular Dx, left ventricle/atrium Dx, MI, ENDOCARDITIS ex. infectious)
  • SYSTEMIC HYPOPERFUSION from "pump failure" (cardiac arrest, arrhythmias) or ↓cardiac output (MI, PE, pericardial effusion, shock...); causes watershed + laminar infarcts

nodes.title: Hyperacute Stroke Management
nodes.body:
• ABCs and vitals incl. glucose: HYPOGLYCEMIA can cause focal neuro/stroke s/s, particularly in setting of old strokes
  • Initiate STROKE PROTOCOL: cardiac monitor, 2 IV lines (one potentially for tPA), labs drawn (see below for Invx needed prior to tPA)
  • Neurologist starts NIH STROKE SCALE (NIHSS) PEx to assess stroke s/s → LOC, gaze, visual field, facial paresis, motor fn, ataxia, sensory, language, dysarthria, extinction → LOCALIZE lesion → imaging

nodes.title: Stroke Protocol Imaging
nodes.body:
• (1) NON-CONTRAST CT HEAD → (2) CT ANGIOGRAM (CTA) HEAD AND NECK → (3) CT PERFUSION (CTP)
  • (1) Non-contrast CT head:
    • Invx for HEMORRHAGE (ICH) ❗ (hyperdense/bright on CT) bc. it's an absolute CI to tPA Tx
    • Invx for ISCHEMIC changes (hypodense/dark on CT) using LOCALIZATION, since change is subtle in first few hrs
  • (2) CTA head and neck:
    • Invx site of LARGE VESSEL OCCLUSION (CTA can't detect small vessels)
    • Invx for AORTIC DISSECTION bc. it's an absolute CI to tPA Tx
    • Invx full CAROTID course for dissection or STENOSIS
  • (3) CT perfusion:
    • Invx for perfusion mismatches: identify salvageable tissue
    • Invx if indications for THROMBECTOMY/EMBOLECTOMY: large mismatch volume on CTP + clot on PROXIMAL LARGE vessel on CTA

nodes.title: Thrombolytic (tPA) Therapy
nodes.body:
• Invx prior to tPA: CT head, CTA, CBC, INR, PTT, glucose, electrolytes
  • CONTRAINDICATIONS: s/s ONSET >4.5 hrs or unwitnessed onset; LARGE INFARCT (>1/3 MCA territory); Hx of ICH or ICH on CT; s/s of SAH; BP >185/110 despite Rx; recent Sx/stroke/GI bleed; ↓Plt; ↑INR/PTT; DOACs <48 hrs
  • If no CIs → rtPA/TNK IV Tx and/or EMBOLECTOMY/THROMBECTOMY if indicated
  • Goal of Tx: re-establish blood flow to ISCHEMIC PENUMBRA (beware hemorrhage post-tPA due to ischemia of downstream vessels)
  • Post-tPA day 1: monitor BP (↑ICH risk if ↑BP), NPO until SLP PEx, 24 hr bed rest, Invx below, PT/OT/social work referral

nodes.title: Invx for Cause of Stroke
nodes.body:
• Telemetry/Holter (ECG) for AFIB
  • Echo for intracardiac thrombus; bubble study for ASD/PFO heart defects
  • CTA or carotid Dopplers for ICA stenosis; CT angiogram for intracranial stenosis
  • CBC for leukocytosis; glucose/lipids/BP for atherosclerosis

nodes.title: Secondary Stroke Prevention
nodes.body:
• Treat underlying cause: if carotid stenosis (>70%) ipsilateral to stroke → ENDARTERECTOMY or stent; if ATRIAL FIBRILLATION or significant VALVE Dx → ANTICOAGULATION (DOAC or warfarin after 2 wks); recall CHADS2
  • Minimize complications w. DVT PROPHYLAXIS (LMWH): balance b/w stroke ↑thrombosis and LMWH ↑hemorrhage risk
  • ANTIPLATELET (ASA ± clopidogrel), BP and glucose control, STATIN
  • ↓modifiable RFs: SMOKING, cocaine use, obesity...
  • Tip box: antiplatelets vs anticoagulants
    • if underlying issue is STASIS of blood (ex. AFIB, DVT, PE, valve Dx) → prevent blood clots with ANTICOAGULANTS (LMWH, DOAC, warfarin)
    • if underlying issue is ENDOTHELIAL INJURY causing platelet activation (ex. ischemia, MI, CAD, ischemic stroke, TIA) → prevent blood clots with ANTIPLATELETS (ASA, clopidogrel)

nodes.title: Classic Stroke Syndromes
nodes.body:
• PEx due to VASCULAR TERRITORIES ⭐ (see UMN lesion localization segment for detailed s/s)
  • Diagram (lateral brain colored by territory + circle of Willis: AComm.A, ICAs, PComA, basilar, vertebral As):
    • ACA: lower limb hemiparesis
    • MCA: aphasia + right face/arm hemiparesis if left MCA; neglect of left side + left face/arm hemiparesis if right MCA
    • PCA: homonymous hemianopia
    • Basilar A. (pons + medulla): crossed sensory s/s, vertigo + other CN-related s/s
  • If MULTIFOCAL CEREBRAL LOCALIZATIONS: #1 possible cause is CARDIOEMBOLIC STROKES; other causes: cerebral vasculitis, multifocal cerebral tumors (more slow onset), multiple cerebral abscesses, demyelination (ex. MS or ADEM)
  • MIMICKERS OF STROKE S/S: migraine AURA (short-duration s/s), TODD'S PARESIS (unwitnessed seizure, s/s improve in hrs), psychogenic (inconsistent s/s if distracted)

nodes.title: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
nodes.body:
• Focal neurological s/s <1 hour, no evidence of acute infarction on imaging
  • Management:
    • (1) CT angiogram (head + neck) or MRI brain to rule out TIA mimics: TUMORS or SUBDURAL HEMATOMA
    • AND other Invx for RFs of TIAs: ECG to Invx for AFIB if s/s of irregular pulse; lipid profile, HbA1c
    • → (2) Start ASA (antiplatelet) ± clopidogrel
    • → (3a) If first TIA: refer to TIA CLINIC to Invx cause of TIA
    • → (3b) If multiple TIAs (i.e. crescendo TIAs): refer to neurology for admission, high risk of STROKE

nodes.title: Cardioembolic Strokes
nodes.body:
• ex. due to AFIB or ENDOCARDITIS
  • If PEx reveals murmur, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots → cause likely ENDOCARDITIS
    • cerebral infarcts prone to 2° HEMORRHAGES ∴ do NOT Tx w. TPA ❗
  • Management: blood cultures x2 for Staph. aureus, enterococcus + slow-growing HACEK organisms; TTE ± TEE; Invx for source of bacteria; if -ve cultures consider non-bacterial endocarditis ex. 2° to malignancy or lupus

nodes.title: Monro-Kellie Hypothesis
nodes.body:
• Intracranial volume = brain + CSF + blood
  • If mass or excess fluid, one of the 3 components ↓ to COMPENSATE; often venous blood ↓ first

nodes.title: High Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
nodes.body:
• NORMAL ICP ≤15 mmHg
  • Etiology: ↑CSF ventriculomegaly, ↑mass from tumor ± peri-lesion edema + vasodilation, ↑blood in hematoma or hemorrhage, infarction + edema, infection, inflammation or abscess, post-hypoxia edema
  • ICP measured w. LUMBAR PUNCTURE (opening pressure), intracranial monitor ± CSF drainage
  • Invx first w. IMAGING (non-contrast CT)

nodes.title: ↑ICP Headaches + S/S
nodes.body:
• May be holocephalic or localized
  • PERSISTENT and PROGRESSIVE
  • POSITIONAL: worse w. supine + worse w. Valsalva or coughing due to ↓venous return to heart → ↑venous blood in brain ↑ICP
  • Worse in MORNINGS + woken up by pain at night due to ↓RR → ↑CO2 (HYPERCAPNIA) during sleep ↑vasodilation in brain → ↑ICP
  • Often associated w. NAUSEA + VOMITING (irritation of trigger zone / area postrema in medulla)
  • PAPILLEDEMA may be visible w. fundoscopy

nodes.title: ↑ICP Red Flags
nodes.body:
• S/S that point to ↑ICP headache:
    • concurrent FEVER + CHILLS (meningitis w. abscess)
    • SUDDEN ONSET of worst headache in life (SAH)
    • 60 pack-year SMOKING Hx (brain metastases)
    • recent head INJURY (hematoma, hemorrhage)
    • FOCAL neurological s/s (stroke)
    • OLDER age, Hx of malignancy, immunosuppression
    • altered LOC + cognition (↓GCS)

nodes.title: Brain Herniation
nodes.body: • MANAGEMENT ⭐: C-spine precaution w. sandbag + collar; head of bed up 30° to ↓central venous pressure; hyperventilation to ↓PaCO2 to ↓brain swelling; IV MANNITOL or 3% NORMAL SALINE for osmotic diuresis (shrinks brain); STAT head NON-CONTRAST CT scan

nodes.title: Subfalcine Herniation
nodes.body: • ↑ICP → cingulate gyrus midline shift → occlusion of ant. cerebral A. → lower limb hemi- or paraparesis

nodes.title: Transtentorial-Uncal Herniation
nodes.body: • ↑ICP → uncus pushed down onto cerebral peduncles + CN III emerging from midbrain → contralateral HEMIPARESIS + ipsilateral PUPIL DILATION (if severe: CN III, IV, VI palsy)

nodes.title: Transtentorial-Central Herniation
nodes.body:
• ↑↑ICP → midbrain pushed down compressing reticular activating system → ↓LOC + COMA
  • PCA + basilar A. occlusion or shearing → vision loss, Duret hemorrhage (pons)

nodes.title: Tonsillar Herniation
nodes.body:
• ↑↑↑ICP → cerebellum pushed into foramen magnum compressing MEDULLA + cardiorespiratory center → CUSHING'S TRIAD ❗⭐:
    • HYPERTENSION (↑BP)
    • BRADYCARDIA (↓HR)
    • DYSPNEA → APNEA SPELLS (↓RR)
  • If untreated → DEATH
  • Why: ↑BP is an attempt to overcome ↑ICP to ↑brain perfusion; ↓HR is a reflex response to ↑BP; irregular RR due to changes at cardioresp. center due to ↑ICP

nodes.title: Broca's Aphasia
nodes.body:
• EXPRESSIVE (speaking or writing)
  • Left MCA, inferior frontal lobe lesion
  • PEx: ↓FLUENCY (↓naming, repetition), normal comprehension

nodes.title: Wernicke's Aphasia
nodes.body:
• RECEPTIVE
  • Left MCA, posterior temporal lobe lesion
  • PEx: ↓COMPREHENSION (↓naming, repetition), normal fluency (but non-sensical)

nodes.title: Global Aphasia
nodes.body:
• Full MCA territory lesion
  • PEx: all language tests ↓

nodes.title: Neglect
nodes.body:
• RIGHT MCA lesions → left body neglect
  • Visual: doesn't attend to R or L visual field
  • Sensory: doesn't attend to R or L sensory stim.
  • Asomatognosia: doesn't recognize own body part
  • Anosognosia: doesn't recognize own sensory deficit

nodes.title: Lesions to Sensory Association Cortex
nodes.body:
• Parietal lobe
  • Graphesthesia: can't identify number/letter written on hand
  • Stereognosia: can't identify object placed in hand
  • Position sensation: can't identify direction of a stimulus

nodes.title: Extinction
nodes.body:
• Can't detect stimuli on affected side if bilateral stimuli presented simultaneously
  • Sensory/light touch (parietal) or visual (occipital)

nodes.title: Cranial Nerves
nodes.body:
• CN UMN: cortex, subcortical tracts, brainstem
  • CN LMN: CN nucleus in brainstem, cranial nerve
  • Most CNs control IPSILATERAL side of face; some have mixed or unique patterns (ex. CN II) ⭐
  • CN 1-12 fiber types: S S M M B M B S B B M M
    • circled green (3, 7, 9, 10) = PARASYMPATHETIC (PSNS) fibers
    • blue * on 5 = "HIGHWAYS" for PSNS (CN V)
  • Head + neck PSNS (intrinsic eye muscles, lacrimal + salivary glands): fibers "hitchhike" ride to target via trigeminal N (V1 and V3*)
  • Diagram (ventral brainstem, CN 1-12 labelled, chiasm): ⭐ PComm.A aneurysms or uncal herniation + CN III compression (arrow to CN III exit)
  • "Rule of 4s" (label at c3/c4 edge): CN 3-4 nuclei in MIDBRAIN; 5-8 nuclei in PONS; 9-12 nuclei in MEDULLA

nodes.title: Cavernous Sinus Lesions
nodes.body:
• Can lead to CN palsies of CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI, as well as orbital pain (via V1) and PROPTOSIS
  • Column 4: the Secondary (provoked) seizures block, febrile seizures, viral encephalitis and the CN I-VI eye innervation segment.
  • Row 3: the dominant / non-dominant / cortical sensory syndrome nodes, Cerebral cortex localization, Hemiplegia, Spinal cord, Central and Posterior cord syndromes.
