  • Possible duplicates: Epilepsy, Cardioembolic strokes and the Rule of 4s label sit on the column 3/4 edge and may also appear in the column-4 transcription.
  • No words were fully illegible.

nodes.title: Secondary (Provoked / Non-Epileptic)
nodes.body:
• ⭐-type asterisk (*): Lesions leave scars / chronic irreversible damage that predisposes pt to seizures (risk >60%)
  • Side note (dashed arrow): Beware of S/S of PSYCHOGENIC seizures

nodes.title: Metabolic (seizure cause)
nodes.body: • ↑/↓ glucose, ↓Ca2+, ↓Na+, uremia, ALCOHOL / drug withdrawal, drug overdose, liver failure...

nodes.title: Fevers (seizure cause)
nodes.body:
• More common in CHILDREN <6 y.o.
  • Most commonly due to VIRAL URTIs

nodes.title: CNS infections (seizure cause)
nodes.body: • * Meningitis, encephalitis, sepsis

nodes.title: Structural (seizure cause)
nodes.body: • * TUMOR, congenital abnormality, AVMs, degenerative (dementia), trauma

nodes.title: Vascular (seizure cause)
nodes.body:
• ICH, SAH, subdural or epidural hematoma
  • * Ischemic STROKE, vasculitis, eclampsia

nodes.title: (Paediatric) Febrile Seizures
nodes.body:
• Children AGE 6 MONTHS - 6 YEARS have lower threshold for seizures ∴ seizures triggered by FEVER >38°C (most commonly due to viral URTI)
  • Note if AGE <6 MONTHS, seizure likely due to MENINGOENCEPHALITIS or sepsis until proven otherwise ❗
  • Diagnosis: fever >38°C + PEx w. NO signs of sepsis or meningoencephalitis or other seizure triggers (ex. hypoglycemia)
  • INVx + MANAGEMENT OF FEBRILE SEIZURES:
    • PEx rules out CNS infection → Hx/PEx to find focus of fever (ex. URTI) → URTI found → no further Invx
    • Hx/PEx does not find URTI → Invx for cause of fever → URINALYSIS (UTIs) + urine culture. No blood cultures.
    • Seizure >15 mins or recurring (>1 in 24 hrs) ∴ COMPLEX seizure → Invx w. EEG/CT/MRI for neurological cause ❗
    • Tx: Tx cause. Antipyretic + fluids for comfort. Prophylactic antipyretics do NOT ↓ recurrence risk.
  • RISK FACTORS FOR RECURRENCE: age onset <18 m.o., FHx in 1st-degree relative, fever <39°C triggering seizure, short fever bf. seizure, COMPLEX febrile seizure, day nursery (↑ viral exposure)

nodes.title: Simple Febrile Seizures
nodes.body:
• Duration: SHORT (<15 mins) + non-recurring
  • Seizure features: GENERALIZED TONIC-CLONIC, no post-ictal S/S
  • Tx: no need for rescue Tx w. benzodiazepines ❗
  • Prognosis: good, very low risk of epilepsy
  • MRI NOT required (may order EEG to confirm seizure was generalized at onset)

nodes.title: Complex Febrile Seizures
nodes.body:
• Duration: LONGER (>15 mins) or RECURRING (>1 in 24 hrs) ❗
  • Seizure features: FOCAL ± generalization. May have TODD'S PARESIS / post-ictal S/S
  • Rescue Tx: BENZODIAZEPINES (lorazepam) used at home in case of emergency (abort seizures >5 mins)
  • Prognosis: ↑ risk of developing EPILEPSY (+↑ risk if FHx, neurodevelopmental impairment); ↑ risk of delayed language + memory impairments
  • Management same as 1st seizure in adult (MRI + EEG)

nodes.title: Beware HPI of Fever + Seizure + Rash in Children
nodes.body:
• ROSEOLA VIRUS (HHV-6): HPI mild FEVER → simple febrile seizure → BLANCHABLE RASH that starts in trunk + neck (usually after the fever ↓). Self-resolves, no other S/S.
  • MENINGOCOCCAL MENINGITIS: HPI mild FEVER + child appears ill (lethargy, ↓feeding, irritability) → ± seizure and NON-BLANCHABLE RASH (PETECHIA or PURPURA) that often starts in lower limbs and spreads. Needs Tx ASAP.

nodes.title: Meningoencephalitis Seizures
nodes.body:
• CNS infections → inflammatory mediators irritate adjacent cerebral cortex → hypersynchronous neuronal activity/seizure. The infection also causes a FEVER, but it is not the fever itself causing the seizure.
  • Red flags: S/S of meningoencephalitis (in children - IRRITABILITY, ↓feeding, bulging fontanelle... see below), neurologic S/S, post-ictal S/S >1 hr, recent ABx, incomplete IMMUNIZATION. Children <6 m.o. w. fever + seizures.

nodes.title: Complications of Meningoencephalitis
nodes.body:
• SEIZURES, especially in CHILDREN
  • CNs exiting through inflamed meninges may be irritated: CN III, IV, VI, VII PALSY
  • Bacterial ABSCESS: S/S of ↑ICP, focal S/S, STROKES, herniation or hydrocephalus: S/S of ↑ICP (see left map) ± Cushing's triad (↑BP, ↓HR, ↓RR), SEPSIS: ↑ or ↓RR, ↓BP, ↑HR
  • ❗ SIADH: ↓Na+, S/S of fluid overload, ↑URINE OUTPUT (inflamm. + ↑ICP lesion to hypothalamus and pituitary gland → ↑ADH release)
  • Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (not covered in PoM II)

nodes.title: Viral (Aseptic) Encephalitis
nodes.body:
• Header note: viruses more likely to invade neurons + brain tissue more than the meninges → encephalitis
  • (May be MENINGOENCEPHALITIS: would also have meningitis PEx)
  • PEx: FEVER, chills, N/V, malaise. Inflammation in brain tissue → ALTERED MENTAL STATUS (lethargy, confusion, focal S/S). If pathogen is HSV (affinity to TEMPORAL LOBES and language areas) → APHASIA S/S ❗. No meningeal irritation ∴ NO NECK STIFFNESS, negative B/K signs.
  • COMMON PATHOGENS:
    • Most important is HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS (HSV) ❗
    • Others: enteroviruses (ex. coxsackievirus), VZV, EBV, CMV, West Nile, HIV...
    • ASEPTIC ENCEPHALITIS (aseptic = -ve CSF culture) less commonly caused by pathogens other than viruses: mycobacteria (TB), spirochetes (LYME and SYPHILIS), fungi ex. cryptococcus, protozoal (NEUROCYSTICERCOSIS), post-infectious, autoimm., toxins, leucemia, IVIg...
  • RFs: exposures ex. babies KISSED by someone w. HSV-1 (oral herpes / COLD SORES)...
  • Tx: IV ACYCLOVIR for HSV encephalitis (started along w. ABx until LP confirms causative agents)
  • After HSV-positive CSF results from LP, Invx to CONFIRM Dx with:
    • EEG: early focal slowing, bilateral TEMPORAL lobe SPIKES
    • MRI: bilateral medial TEMPORAL LOBE NECROSIS (Klüver-Bucy syndrome)
    • If Dx still unclear after non-invasive Invx, consider BIOPSY
  • From viral CSF result: Stop empirical ABx; continue acyclovir if HSV confirmed. If -ve for HSV (and VZV) stop acyclovir: ❗ HYDRATION + SUPPORTIVE Tx only (non-HSV viral encephalitis and/or meningitis)

nodes.title: Viral Meningitis
nodes.body:
• PEx: similar to bacterial meningitis but often milder (ex. NO SEIZURES), pt is "less ill"
  • S/S also milder than viral encephalitis, does not cause S/S associated w. temporal lobe
  • Self-resolving

nodes.title: Management of Meningoencephalitis
nodes.body:
• Same approach in meningitis + encephalitis as they often have similar PEx or co-exist as meningoencephalitis
  • 1. ABCs, cardioresp monitor, IV lines...
  • 2. BLOOD labs: CBC + diff, glucose (will be compared to CSF glucose), CRP, INR + PTT (especially if petechiae), lytes (monitor Na+ for SIADH), BUN/Cr, blood CULTURE + urine sample if possible: culture
  • 3. START TREATMENT: EMPIRIC ABx (ceftriaxone + vanco) ⭐, ampicillin if >50 y.o., dexamethasone + ACYCLOVIR for HSV (in a perfect world ABx after LP, but there are delays in CT + LP)
  • 4. Examine for MASS LESIONS (↑ICP) that would cause herniation during a lumbar puncture: most commonly w. CT SCAN of head ❗
    • Contraindications to LP without prior CT: PAPILLEDEMA or poorly visualized fundus, abnormal LOC, focal S/S, seizure, Hx of CNS Dx, immunocompromised or other RFs for ↑ICP...
    • If clear CT scan (or absolute certainty of normal ICP) and no other contraindications to LP (ex. coagulopathy) ↓
  • 5. LUMBAR PUNCTURE + CSF LABS
    • Viral (mainly lymphocytes): cell count mild ↑WBCs (<1,000); glucose normal (CSF:serum >0.6); proteins mild ↑; culture + Gram stain ⊖ / normal (aseptic); viral PCR ⊕ for HSV or other virus; CSF appearance normal or bloody; LP opening pressure normal (<25)
    • Bacterial (mainly neutrophils): cell count ↑↑WBCs (500-50,000); glucose ↓ (CSF:serum ratio <0.3); proteins ↑↑ high; culture + Gram stain ⊕; viral PCR ⊖ for HSV + other viruses; CSF appearance pus; LP opening pressure ↑↑ (>30)
      • → Adjust ABx based on CSF culture + sensitivity results (→ Bacterial meningitis Tx)
  • + Monitor for COMPLICATIONS (ex. hyponatremia due to SIADH)

nodes.title: Bacterial Meningitis (Aka Acute Purulent meningitis)
nodes.body:
• Header note: bacteria more likely to colonize the meninges + ↑inflammation via toxins → meningitis
  • PEx of OLDER CHILDREN + ADULTS: FEVER (immunocompromised pt may not have fever), meningeal irritation: around the brain → HEADACHE, around the brainstem → NECK STIFFNESS (nuchal rigidity) and around the lumbar/sacral spinal cord → positive BRUDZINSKI'S + KERNIG'S SIGN (see CalgaryGuide.com for MOA). Inflammation near brain ↓function: ALTERED MENTAL STATUS (lethargy, confusion, focal S/S, photophobia, N/V, if ↑ICP: papilledema). If pathogen is meningococcus → infects endothelium of lower limbs → PETECHIAL or PURPURIC RASH (non-blanchable) ❗
  • PEx of NEONATES + CHILDREN: FEVER, paradoxic IRRITABILITY (baby irritated if moved), lethargy, vomiting, poor feeding, bulging of ANTERIOR FONTANELLE. Brudzinski and Kernig's sign less specific in pt <1 y.o. ± petechial RASH.
  • COMMON PATHOGENS (Gram +ve in purple, Gram -ve in pink):
    • NEONATES + CHILDREN <3 m.o. (RF: colonized from mom in VAGINAL BIRTH): Group B Streptococcus; E. coli
    • EVERYONE (RF: UNVACCINATED) ❗: Strep. pneumoniae (pneumococcus); Haemophilus influenzae; Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus) w. petechial or purpuric RASH ... "Gram-ve diplococci"
    • PT. W. SPECIFIC RFs: Listeria if >50 y.o.; Staph. aureus if head trauma or Sx
  • RFs: recent infections (URTI, otitis media, sinusitis, UTIs...), IMMUNODEFICIENCY (HIV, ASPLENIA - review FoM week 15 map), chronic Dx, sickle cell Dx, CNS trauma, cochlear implant, VP shunt, CSF leak, travel, exposures, sick contacts (ex. daycare)
    • → NEONATES (0-1 y.o.) w. FEVER but without an obvious source of infection will have a LUMBAR PUNCTURE as part of full-sepsis workup to Invx for meningitis as cause of fever due to their ↑ risk (review from FoM week 15 map: sepsis)
  • Tx: CEFTRIAXONE + VANCOMYCIN. If >50 y.o. or immunocompromised: AMPICILLIN for Listeria coverage. + DEXAMETHASONE (significant ↓ in morbidity - hearing loss, and mortality, of Strep. pneumo. meningitis). ABx + steroids + ACYCLOVIR for HSV until LP confirms.

nodes.title: Brain Death
nodes.body:
• (−) alertness and awareness, (−) primitive reflexes
  • Established etiology, deep unresponsive coma with absent brainstem reflexes, absent respiratory effort on apnea test, absent confounding factors

nodes.title: Coma
nodes.body:
• (−) alertness and awareness, (+) primitive reflexes only, (−) sleep-wake cycles. Pt is not dead.
  • Causes: global cortical dysfunction (ex. hypoxic-ischemic injury, toxic, trauma...), bi-thalamic or hypothalamic lesion (ex. basilar stroke), BRAINSTEM (RETICULAR) LESION (ex. stroke, HERNIATION syndromes...)
  • Treatable causes: shock (↓BP), ↓BG, DKA, toxins, meningitis, HSV encephalitis, brain abscess, epi- or sub-dural hematoma, HTN encephalopathy

nodes.title: Vegetative State
nodes.body:
• (aka unresponsive wakefulness syndrome)
  • (+) alertness, (−) awareness, (+) primitive reflexes AND non-purposeful reflexive movements, (+) sleep-wake cycles

nodes.title: MCS (−)
nodes.body: • WITHOUT command following

nodes.title: Minimally Conscious State (MCS)
nodes.body: • (+) alertness, (+) awareness, minimal level of behavioural interactions, (−) functional communication

nodes.title: Emergence From MCS
nodes.body:
• (+) functional communication and object use
  • Progression to normal consciousness

nodes.title: Disorders of Consciousness
nodes.body: • (label bar only)

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Altered Level of Consciousness
nodes.body:
• Components of consciousness: ALERTNESS / WAKEFULNESS (arousal) and AWARENESS (content)
  • Maintained by: 1. ascending RETICULAR ACTIVATING SYSTEM (RAS) in the upper PONS + MIDBRAIN; 2. projections through THALAMUS into 3. wide areas of CEREBRAL CORTEX

nodes.title: Other Alterations
nodes.body:
• LOCKED-IN SYNDROME (mimics coma)
  • Transient loss of consciousness: syncope, seizures... (see map segment left of seizures)
  • Impaired awareness: ENCEPHALOPATHY / DELIRIUM

nodes.title: Assess Mental Status in PEx
nodes.body:
• 1. Observe + interact: alert, drowsy, stuporous, somnolent, obtunded, comatose
  • 2. Oriented to "person" (Q: name, DOB), "place" (Q: where are you), and "time" (year, day of week)

nodes.title: Assessment of Unconscious Patients
nodes.body: • General observations: responsiveness, agitation, movements, automatisms, breathing, fundoscopy for ICP, GCS SCORE

nodes.title: CRANIAL NERVE PEx (unconscious pt)
nodes.body:
• Pupil Ex + pupillary light reflex: blown pupils (CN III compression / uncal herniation), miosis/small pupils (Horner syndrome / brainstem or cord lesion), CN II (RAPD)
  • Ocular motor Ex (CN III, IV, VI):
    • 1. Observation: fixed deviation, bobbing, nystagmus
    • 2. Eye movements to command (if any): gaze limitations w. specific CN dysfunction
    • 3. OCULOCEPHALIC "DOLL'S EYES" REFLEX: head movement inputs via CN VIII; in an abnormal Ex the eyes will stay fixed w. head (instead of moving relative to the head)
    • 4. VESTIBULO-OCULAR REFLEX: saline water into ear, input via CN VIII → normal response is "COWS" - cold opposite, warm same. Comatose pt will have slow deviation towards same side as cold.
  • Corneal reflex (CN V and VII) and gag/cough reflex (CN IX and X) - often last reflex lost

nodes.title: SENSORY/MOTOR PEx (unconscious pt)
nodes.body:
• Tone + spontaneous movement / command following (if any)
  • Painful stimuli: central (ex. sternum) + peripheral (ex. nail-bed pressure). Look for response ex. grimacing, withdraws...
  • Deep tendon reflexes (asymmetry, ↑ or ↓), plantar responses (flexor/down, extensor/up/Babinski, absent) and POSTURING REFLEXES (in response to central pain stimulus):
    • DECORTICATE POSTURING: "flexor" posturing, pyramidal pattern of weakness ⭐. FLEXION of upper limb, EXTENSION of lower limb. Lesions in BRAIN (above midbrain)
    • DECEREBRATE POSTURING: "extensor" posturing, pyramidal pattern in lower limb ⭐. EXTENSION of both upper and lower limb. Lesions lower in BRAINSTEM
    • Triple flexion: flexion of hip, knee + ankle. Spinal cord reflex.

nodes.title: Neuroradiology
nodes.body:
• CT: ↑ density (ex. bone and blood) = white
  • T2 MRI: ↑ fluid (ex. edema and necrosis) = white
  • In neurorad, CONTRAST helps show breakdown of BBB, ex. due to infection/inflammation, angiogenesis by tumors or hemorrhage (contrast exits blood → enters CSF, meninges, tissue)
  • COMMON INVESTIGATIONS:
    • Hemorrhages, strokes, hydrocephalus: NON-CONTRAST CT SCANS: acute blood is hyperdense/bright. Edema and necrosis i.e. infarcts are hypodense/dark (visible few hrs after stroke). → CT angiogram + CT perfusion used in stroke protocol
    • Tumors: T2 MRI w. CONTRAST: tumors often enhancing/bright (breakdown BBB). → If MRI unavailable, CONTRAST-ENHANCED CT for tumors: hypodense/dark with enhancing regions
    • Multiple sclerosis: T2 MRI w. FLAIR (attenuates CSF signal): demyelinated plaques appear hyperintense/bright, often paraventricular location
    • Meningoencephalitis + 2° Invx for subarachnoid hemorrhage + MS: CSF via LUMBAR PUNCTURE + almost always needs PRIOR CT HEAD: cell count/glucose... for infections, xanthochromia/Hg for SAH, IgG for MS
    • Seizures/epilepsy, sleep Dx, coma: ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAM (EEG): abnormal ↑ spikes during seizures
    • LMN localized lesions: ELECTROMYOGRAM (EMG) + NERVE CONDUCTION STUDIES: used for diabetic neuropathy, GBS, MG, ALS, myopathies, radiculopathy...
  • OTHER LESS COMMON NEURORAD INVx:
    • T1 MRI: anatomy, CSF is dark
    • T2 MRI without contrast: CSF and pathologies - bright ("WWII - water is white in T2")
    • Susceptibility weighted (SWI) T2 MRI: detects chronic/old bleeds (hemosiderin) - hypointense/dark
    • Diffusion weighted (DWI) T2 MRI: early detection of ischemic changes/stroke - hyperintense/bright
    • Doppler U/S for internal carotid A. stenosis. Does NOT visualize vertebral A. (ex. not for Invx of brainstem-only lesion)

nodes.title: Neurological Disorders
nodes.body:
• COMMON PRESENTATIONS: weakness, sensory deficits, gait disturbances/unsteadiness, ataxia, dizziness/vertigo, ptosis, aphasia, dysarthria, neglect, headaches, altered level of consciousness, seizures, loss of consciousness, cognitive impairment
  • DESCRIPTION OF HPI: in addition to localization, begin DIFFERENTIAL Dx during Hx by determining ONSET (acute, subacute, chronic), COURSE (progressive, intermittent, stable) + associated deficits (ex. OCULAR S/S, FACIAL DROOP, BLADDER/BOWEL...)
  • ONSET:
    • HYPERACUTE (seconds-hrs) → STROKE, migraine aura, trauma
    • ACUTE (hrs-days) → infection, inflammation
    • SUBACUTE (wks-6 months) → TUMOR, toxic, chronic subdural hematoma
    • CHRONIC (6 months-yrs) → degenerative, hereditary
  • NOMENCLATURE: Hemi- = half body (R/L face, arm, leg); Quadri- = all 4 limbs; Para- = both lower limbs; -plegia = paralysis; -paresis = weakness; Ataxia = ↓coordination ex. unsteadiness; Antalgia = ↓movement/position due to pain; Dysarthria = difficulty w. articulation; Dysmetria = difficulty reaching target; Bulbar = medulla (bulb-shaped); Myel- = spinal cord or marrow; Spondy- = spinal column vertebrae; Pyramidal = UMN in cerebral cortex; Extra-pyramidal = basal ganglia
  • ABBREVIATIONS: RHD right hand dominant; EOM extraocular movements; PERLA pupils equal and reactive to light and accommodation; FTN finger-to-nose; HTS heel-to-shin; RAM rapid alternating movements; DTR deep tendon reflexes; OD right eye, OS left eye, OU both eyes

nodes.title: Concussion
nodes.body:
• Mild TRAUMATIC head injury (rotational acceleration), DIFFUSELY, without focal neurological deficits
  • RFs: young age (↑ recovery time), females, Hx of concussion
  • PEx: HEADACHE, dizziness, nausea, imbalance, "seeing stars"...
  • Diagnosis: CLINICAL Dx (no specific Invx or imaging). Use of Qs ex. SCAT5. Only need ONE S/S to Dx.
  • Red flags: neck pain, double vision, weakness or sensory S/S, seizure, loss of consciousness, GCS <15, vomiting, worsening S/S
  • Tx: REST 24-48 hrs until free of S/S. Gradual return to activities.
  • Prognosis: 85% of 1st concussion will fully recover in 1-4 weeks
  • If return to activities too early or repeated concussions:
    • Second-impact syndrome or post-traumatic cerebral swelling
    • Post-concussion syndrome (S/S >4 wks), permanent remove from play
    • Post-traumatic epilepsy, psychological Dx (ex. depression...)
    • CHRONIC TRAUMATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY: athletes w. Hx of repeat concussions → tau-positive neurofibrillary tangles, brain degeneration → chronic headaches, psych. S/S, DEMENTIA, movement Dx, suicide... → Dx at autopsy (neuropath. Dx)

nodes.title: Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
nodes.body:
• (FOCAL neurological S/S "SEPARATED IN TIME AND SPACE")
  • Epidemiology: most common in Caucasian YOUNG FEMALES (age of onset 20-40 y.o., F:M ratio 3:1)
  • Pathophys: genetics (HLA DRB1), ↓VITAMIN D (ex. Canadians), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), SMOKING, obesity, shiftwork → AUTOIMMUNE attack of OLIGODENDROCYTES myelin sheath via T/B cells + ↑ OLIGOCLONAL IgG → "PATCHY DEMYELINATION" → slow signal conduction (RELAPSING). S/S depend on site of lesion (cortical, OPTIC NERVE, PARAVENTRICULAR, brainstem, spinal cord...) → acute lesions are REMYELINATED after wks-months ∴ S/S improve (REMITTING). If lesions are chronic, axonal degeneration → axonal sclerosis (plaques) → permanent deficits (PROGRESSIVE)
  • Clinical subtypes: RELAPSING-REMITTING MS (most common, ex. young female) → with age most become: 2° PROGRESSIVE MS (ex. older females). Others: 1° progressive MS (ex. older males) without relapses.
  • PEx: lesion in spinal cord (myelitis) → sensory S/S + WEAKNESS w. UMN PEx, bladder + bowel S/S. OPTIC NEURITIS → RAPD, visual deficits. Brainstem lesion → diplopia, impaired gait, vertigo... etc. S/S peak over days-wks, followed by variable improvement over wks-months.
  • Invx: T2-weighted MRI SCAN w. FLAIR showing demyelinating plaques (hyperintense/BRIGHT lesions), typically paraventricular ex. "DAWSON'S FINGERS" - paraventricular lesions extending into corpus callosum ❗. ± LUMBAR PUNCTURE to Invx CSF: presence of OLIGOCLONAL BANDS - ↑IgG concentration in most MS pt.
  • Diagnosis: focal neurological S/S disseminated in TIME (≥2 attacks with 30 days b/w attacks, w. simultaneous findings on MRI or LP) + SPACE (lesions on MRI in ≥2 CNS regions)
  • Tx: acute Tx → CORTICOSTEROIDS. Disease-modifying Tx → many new Tx ex. INTERFERON-β. Symptomatic Tx → Tx specific S/S ex. pain w. TCA, gabapentin, erectile dysfunction w. Viagra... etc.

nodes.title: Nutritional Deficiencies + Toxic Injuries
nodes.body:
• Vitamin B6 toxicity → sensory neuropathy; COPPER deficiency → myelopathy
  • RE-FEEDING SYNDROME: pt w. prolonged caloric depletion → re-feeding too fast → ↑↑↑ insulin → intracellular shift → ↓Na+, ↓K+, ↓Ca2+, ↓Mg2+, ↓PO4 3- → encephalopathy (confusion, unsteadiness), weakness → if severe: SEIZURES and cardiac arrhythmias

nodes.title: Vitamin B12 Deficiency
nodes.body:
• Subacute combined degeneration: encephalopathy → DEMENTIA (↓memory, ↓personality, ↓cognition...), peripheral neuropathy → paresthesias... and MYELOPATHY - degeneration of POSTERIOR SPINAL CORD / dorsal column → SENSORY (GAIT) ATAXIA (see etiology of posterior cord syndrome)
  • The peripheral neuropathy also contributes to sensory ataxia (see Ataxia below)
  • Do not miss Dx, easy to Invx and Tx ❗
  • Reversible causes of DEMENTIA: major depressive disorder, thyroid disease, neurosyphilis + Vit. B12 deficiency

nodes.title: Vitamin B1 aka Thiamine Deficiency
nodes.body: • ex. due to CHRONIC ALCOHOLISM

nodes.title: Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome
nodes.body:
• (Acute = Wernicke's encephalopathy, chronic = Korsakoff's psychosis w. atrophy of mamillary bodies ∴ AMNESIA + confabulation)
  • WERNICKE'S ENCEPHALOPATHY PEx TRIAD:
    • Confusion / COGNITIVE impairment
    • OPHTHALMOPARESIS (ex. bilateral CN VI palsy)
    • BILATERAL CEREBELLAR ATAXIA
  • Can be triggered by REFEEDING of pt in starvation mode w.o. proper thiamine supplementation (PREVENT by giving thiamine BEFORE glucose in pt w. suspected nutritional deficits ex. alcoholics, eating disorder, elderly...)
    • → In the wards, IV thiamine may be known as "Banana Bags" (yellow)
  • Wernicke's is largely REVERSIBLE vs. Korsakoff's syndrome is largely irreversible

nodes.title: Dry/Wet Beri-Beri Syndrome
nodes.body:
• Sensorimotor PERIPHERAL neuropathy
  • Wet beri-beri has associated cardiomyopathy

nodes.title: Sympathetics
nodes.body:
• Tracts do not decussate ∴ innervate IPSILATERAL face/body
  • Nuclei in HYPOTHALAMUS → descend via PONS + MEDULLA (possible lesion site via pontine arteries)
  • → Thoracic spinal cord (C8-T2): common site of lesion is fibers exiting at C8/T1 (ex. C8 radiculopathy) causing Horner's syndrome
  • → SUPERIOR CERVICAL GANGLION: travel w. branches of INTERNAL CAROTID A. (+CN V near target)
  • Targets: ↑ SWEAT GLANDS; VASOCONSTRICTION (which in turn ↓ secretion of salivary glands); superior tarsal muscle (minor EYELID LIFTER); DILATOR PUPILLAE (pupil dilation)

nodes.title: CN I: Olfactory N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers: S. sensory - smell
  • Foramina: cribriform plate of ethmoid
  • Cell bodies: olfactory epithelium

nodes.title: CN II: Optic N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers: S. sensory - vision (pupil light reflex / RAPD afferent)
  • Foramina: optic canal
  • Cell bodies: retina
  • Covered w. dura mater ∴ meningitis can spread

nodes.title: CN VI: Abducens N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers: motor - lateral rectus
  • Cell bodies (nucleus): pons (pons-medulla landmark)
  • Foramina: superior orbital fissure

nodes.title: CN IV: Trochlear N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers: motor - superior oblique
  • Cell bodies (nucleus): midbrain (posterior, long course - vulnerable to trauma)
  • Foramina: superior orbital fissure

nodes.title: CN III: Oculomotor N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers: motor - EOM; PSNS - pupil constriction, lens accommodation
  • Cell bodies (nucleus): midbrain - motor, PSNS pre-synap. neuron in Edinger-Westphal nucleus
  • Foramina: superior orbital fissure
  • Cell bodies (ganglion): PSNS post-synap. in CILIARY GANGLION

nodes.title: CN III / V1 / V2 eye-innervation diagram
nodes.body:
• CN III (motor) → LEVATOR PALPEBRAE SUPERIORIS (main EYELID LIFTER) and SR, IR, MR, IO extrinsic eye muscles
  • CN III (PSNS) (RAPD efferent - bilateral) → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves → SPHINCTER PUPILLAE (pupil constriction), CILIARY MUSCLE (lens accommodation)
  • Ophthalmic N. (V1) (gen. sensory) → nasociliary N. → long ciliary N. ← gen. sensory from cornea (corneal reflex afferent); infratrochlear N.
  • V1 → frontal N. → supraorbital N., supratrochlear N.
  • V1 → lacrimal N. → LACRIMAL GLAND (PSNS from pterygopalatine ganglion carried via zygomatic N.: "in PT fossa to orbit via inf. orbital fissure")
  • Maxillary N. (V2) (gen. sensory) → infraorbital N.; zygomatic N.; pterygopalatine ganglion

nodes.title: V1: Ophthalmic
nodes.body:
• Fibers: gen. sensory - forehead/eyes/nose + corneal reflex sens.
  • Foramina: superior orbital fissure
  • Highway to PSNS of intrinsic eye muscles + lacrimal gland from CN III + VII

nodes.title: CN V: Trigeminal N.
nodes.body:
• Fibers: sensory (all) + motor (V3)
  • Function: gen. sensory to face, mastication
  • Cell bodies: pons (sensory nucleus spans all brainstem + trigeminal ganglion)
  • → TRIGEMINAL NEURALGIA (+ varicella zoster reactivation)

nodes.title: V3: Mandibular
nodes.body:
• Fibers: gen. sens - jaw, lower lip, ant 2/3 tongue; motor - mastication
  • Foramina: F. ovale. Travels into infratemporal fossa.
  • Highway to parotid gland PSNS (CN IX) + chorda tympani (CN VII) w. taste to ant 2/3 of tongue + PSNS to submandibular glands

nodes.title: V2: Maxillary
nodes.body:
• Fibers: gen. sens - cheeks/upper lip
  • Foramina: F. rotundum. Travels into pterygopalatine (PT) fossa.

nodes.title: "Rule of 4s"
nodes.body:
• CN 3, 4: nuclei in MIDBRAIN
  • CN 5, 6, 7, 8: nuclei in PONS
  • CN 9, 10, 11, 12: nuclei in MEDULLA
  • (CN 1, 2 labelled above, no nucleus group)

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Ptosis (Droopy Eyelids)
nodes.body:
• NON-NEUROLOGICAL CAUSES: congenital; excess skin (dermatochalasis); levator dehiscence
  • Localization to MUSCLES: hereditary myopathies (proximal weakness, see LMN)
  • Localization to NMJ: MYASTHENIA GRAVIS (FLUCTUATING weakness, worse at END OF DAY, see LMN)
  • Localization to NERVE or BRAINSTEM/CORD: ptosis + ANISOCORIA: unequal pupil sizes (normal pupil diameter is 2-4 mm in bright light, 4-8 mm in dark)

nodes.title: Horner's Syndrome
nodes.body:
• Etiology: brainstem or spinal cord lesion to SNS tracts, lesion to fibers along INTERNAL CAROTID A. (ex. by a mediastinum mass...)
  • Clinical presentation ⭐:
    • CONSTRICTED PUPIL (aka MIOSIS)
    • Ptosis (less severe than CN III palsy, superior tarsal muscle has minor role in lifting eyelids, unlike LPS by CN III) → note eyes will be directed normally
    • Flushing (vasodilation)
    • Anhydrosis
    • (S/S are IPSILATERAL to side of lesion)

nodes.title: CN III Compression
nodes.body:
• Etiology: P Comm A. aneurysm, uncal herniation (tumor, stroke, hemorrhage), ischemic (DM), cavernous sinus lesions
  • Clinical presentation: fixed + DILATED PUPIL (aka MYDRIASIS) "BLOWN PUPIL"; ptosis due to LPS paralysis; down and out position due to EOM → CN III (+ IV, VI) palsy → DIPLOPIA
  • CN III LESION PATTERNS ⭐:
    • PSNS fibers run along outside of nerve → COMPRESSIVE LESION (ex. uncal herniation): blown pupil (MYDRIASIS)
    • Somatic motor fibers and nerve VASCULATURE run along center of nerve → ISCHEMIC LESION (ex. diabetic CN III neuropathy): reactive pupil (PUPIL SPARING); ptosis + down/out position/diplopia

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Diplopia (Double Vision)
nodes.body:
• Due to OCULAR MISALIGNMENT aka STRABISMUS from WEAKNESS of ≥1 EXTRINSIC EYE MUSCLE
  • Localizes to BRAINSTEM (CN III, IV, VI nuclei lesions, ex. WERNICKE'S encephalopathy), cranial nerves (CN PALSY, see below), NMJ (MYASTHENIA GRAVIS), or eye muscles (GRAVE'S Dx, trauma...)
  • ⭐ but NEVER due to lesions ROSTRAL to the BRAINSTEM ❗
  • Direction of deviation: esotropia inward; exotropia outward; hypertropia upward; hypotropia downward

nodes.title: CN Palsies W. EOM Deficits
nodes.body:
• (Diagrams depict the anterior view of the RIGHT EYE only)
  • EOM ACTIONS (lateral on left, medial on right): IO3 up-lateral, LR6 lateral, SO4 down-lateral; SR3 up-medial, MR3 medial, IR3 down-medial. Points A (on SO), B (on MR), C (on SR) mark palsy eye positions.
  • (o A,B,C) CN PALSY EYE POSITIONS, due to unopposed action of balancing muscles:
    • A. CN III palsy (aneurysm, herniations) (+ ptosis + dilated pupils), due to unopposed LR and SO (dashed → CN III compression)
    • B. CN VI palsy (tumors w. ↑ICP), due to unopposed MR, compensate w. head TURN (dashed → "Anytime there's signs of a CN VI palsy, Invx for PAPILLEDEMA + other signs of ↑ICP ❗")
    • C. CN IV palsy (trauma, congenital), due to unopposed SR, compensate w. head TILT
  • EXTRINSIC EYE MUSCLES' ATTACHMENTS (diagram: SR, SO, LR, MR (medial/nasal), IR, IO): SO + IO insert posteriorly; SO inserts via the trochlea
  • EOM TESTING (lateral left / medial right): SR up-lateral, LR6 lateral, IR down-lateral; IO up-medial, MR medial, SO4 down-medial. Test SO by moving eye medial, then down: IR "busy" w. medial adduction, only muscle that can ↓ eye is SO.
  • Note that STRABISMUS in adults → diplopia VS strabismus in CHILDREN → strabismic AMBLYOPIA

nodes.title: Paediatric Amblyopia (Aka "Lazy Eye")
nodes.body:
• Progressive suppression of visual input / ↓ visual cortex development (∴ VISION LOSS) from eye receiving suboptimal image
  • Types:
    • STRABISMIC AMBLYOPIA (concomitant/non-paralytic or incomitant/paralytic/restrictive due to CN PALSY, orbital trauma, or thyroid ophthalmopathy)
    • REFRACTIVE AMBLYOPIA
    • FORM-DEPRIVATION + OCCLUSION AMBLYOPIA
  • MANAGEMENT: Invx corneal light reflexes, cover/uncover test, red reflex asymmetry. Tx: PATCH THE GOOD EYE, glasses, Sx. Refer if constant deviation or occasional in 4 mo+.

nodes.title: Localization of Visual Field Deficits
nodes.body:
• VISUAL PROCESSING (diagram): left visual field (T, C) red; right visual field (C, T) blue; T = temporal hemifield, C = central hemifield; optic nerve (CN II) → optic chiasm → LGN (thalamus) → optic radiations → Right 1° VISUAL CORTEX (occipital lobe)
    • 4 Upper bank: Right inferior visual field (as written)
    • 5 Lower bank: Right superior v. field (as written)
    • 6 Tip of occipital lobe: macula/fovea
    • ↓↓ Parietal: dorsal/"where" stream; Temporal: ventral/"what" stream
    • Nasal hemiretina fibers DECUSSATE at optic chiasm (detect temporal visual fields) vs. temporal hemiretina does not
    • Visual field info is detected in contralateral visual cortex
    • Some CN II fibers go to: EDINGER-WESTPHAL NUCLEUS (MIDBRAIN): presynaptic PSNS cell bodies of CN III/oculomotor → bilateral (both eyes) PSNS efferent via CN III: CONSENSUAL PUPIL CONSTRICTION ⭐
    • If CN II lesion (1) is suspected, Invx w. SWINGING FLASHLIGHT TEST for a RELATIVE AFFERENT PUPILLARY DEFECT (RAPD): pupil w. CN II lesion will DILATE in response to flashlight
  • LESION LOCALIZATION ❗:
    • 1. CN II: R. MONOCULAR vision loss / ANOPSIA
    • 2. Optic chiasm: BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA
    • 3. R. optic tract: L. HOMONYMOUS HEMIANOPIA
    • 4. L. homonymous inferior quadrantanopia
    • 5. L. homonymous superior quadrantanopia
    • 6. L. homonymous SCOTOMA
    • 7. L. homonymous macular-sparing hemianopia
    • (each with drawn left/right eye field icons)

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Monocular Vision Loss
nodes.body: • Invx: visual acuity (VA), swinging flashlight, red reflex, TONOMETRY (for IOP), fundoscopy, visual fields

nodes.title: Chronic Vision Loss
nodes.body:
• OPEN-ANGLE GLAUCOMA:
    • RFs: FHx, ↑age, Black, myopia, ↑IOP, Hx of steroids, vasospasms, ocular trauma
    • Pathophys: ↓ in aqueous outflow due to ↓ flow in trabecular venous meshwork ± ↑IOP (normal is 10-21 mmHg) → optic nerve head damage → CUP:DISK RATIO ↑ (normal is <0.5) → slow ↓ PERIPHERAL VISION ❗
    • Tx: ↓IOP via drops, laser or Sx
  • AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION (ARMD):
    • PEx: DRUSEN (lipid deposits) in both types, ❗ ↓ CENTRAL VISION, metamorphopsia (distortion)
    • DRY ARMD: retinal ATROPHY in macula, moderate ↓vision. Could progress to wet. Tx w. lifestyle (nutrition, ↓smoking)...
    • WET ARMD: sub-retinal HEMORRHAGE in macula → may have sudden severe ↓vision. Tx w. ANTI-VEGF intraocular injections.
  • CATARACTS:
    • Opacity and discoloration of lens → ↓VA
    • Types: nuclear sclerosis, post. subcapsular, cortical
    • Tx: lens replacement Sx
    • links: dotted ← "Opaque" (abnormal red reflex)

nodes.title: Abnormal Red Reflex
nodes.body:
• Opaque → cataracts / vitreous hemorrhage
  • Asymmetric: many causes ex. STRABISMUS
  • White aka LEUKOKORIA → must rule out RETINOBLASTOMA: malignant ocular tumor in CHILDREN (FHx likely if bilateral)

nodes.title: Amaurosis Fugax
nodes.body: • TEMPORARY and brief loss of vision due to transient ↓ blood flow to retina, ex. due to carotid or AFib embolus. May precede a STROKE.

nodes.title: Acute Vision Loss
nodes.body:
• (Sudden ↓↓VA, ↓ or no pupil response to light directly)
  • PAINLESS:
    • W.O. CLEAR MEDIA (± dull red reflex) → VITREOUS HEMORRHAGE: most common cause is DIABETIC RETINOPATHY (DR). PROLIFERATIVE DR: neovascularization/fragile new vessels → bleeding into vitrous humor. Tx: laser Tx.
    • W. CLEAR MEDIA (± clear red reflex) → chain: CRAO → ION → GCA → Optic neuritis → Retinal detachment

nodes.title: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)
nodes.body:
• Thrombus or atherosclerotic plaque dislodges from carotid A. branches
  • PEx: CHERRY-RED MACULAR SPOT + RAPD, white opacity retina
  • Tx: ophth. EMERGENCY. Immediate Tx w. eye compressions 10s for 5 mins.

nodes.title: Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (ION)
nodes.body: • Etiology: non-arteritic ION due to HTN, DM, Viagra... Arteritic ION due to GCA →

nodes.title: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA)
nodes.body:
• PEx: new HEADACHE in >50 y.o. pt, TEMPORAL A. tender, JAW pain, ± PMR S/S... see Rheum map. +ve RAPD, FLAME-shaped hemorrhages.
  • Invx: ↑ESR, CRP. Tx w. HIGH-DOSE STEROIDS ASAP. Emergent referral to ophtho.

nodes.title: Optic Neuritis
nodes.body:
• Etiology: suspect MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS if YOUNG FEMALE ❗, other inflammatory and infectious ex. neuromyelitis optica
  • PEx: +RAPD, OPTIC NERVE SWELLING on retinal exam
  • VS bilateral optic N./disc swelling also seen in PAPILLEDEMA caused by ↑ICP: DDx by looking for other S/S of ↑ICP

nodes.title: Retinal Detachment
nodes.body:
• PEx: FLASHING LIGHTS (photopsia) → new-onset FLOATERS - black dots, may be RBCs due to tear ❗ → ↓ PERIPHERAL VISION
  • Tx: refer ophtho for Sx reattachment

nodes.title: Clinical Approach to Red Eyes
nodes.body: • Invx: fluorescein dye for corneal abrasions + for SEIDEL TEST (to detect leaks through cornea), SLIT LAMP (for detailed Ex of anterior eye), CHAMBER DEPTH (↓ depth w. angle closure), red reflex

nodes.title: Painful = Vision Threatening
nodes.body:
• (Acute painful red eyes w. vision loss / ↓VA)
  • CORNEAL ULCERS: BACTERIAL KERATITIS ❗(red flag)
    • (corneal abrasion → infected cornea → ulcer)
    • PEx: ↑ risk if CONTACT LENSES, CORNEAL HAZE, CILIARY FLUSH, inflamm. cells in ant. chamber, severe pain, corneal opacity, pus + HYPOPION
    • Tx: stop contact lens use. Refer to ophth. ABx.
  • IRITIS aka ANTERIOR UVEITIS ❗(red flag)
    • May be HLA B27 associated, ± S/S of SPONDYLOARTHRITIS (review Rheum map), but 50% are idiopathic
    • PEx: CILIARY FLUSH, ↓VA, PHOTOPHOBIA, severe pain ❗, cells + flare in ant. chamber ± KERATOPRECIPITATES, ± Hx of past episode, back pain, morning stiffness...
    • Tx: urgent ophth. referral for STEROID DROPS - should ONLY be prescribed by ophthos. ± Rheum ref.
  • ACUTE ANGLE CLOSURE GLAUCOMA ❗(red flag)
    • RFs: FHx, ↑age, Asian, females, hyperopia
    • Pathophys: acute/rapid onset ↓ in aqueous outflow due to blockage of drainage angle → RAPID ↑↑IOP ❗
    • PEx: SHALLOW ANTERIOR CHAMBER DEPTH, corneal edema, "ROCK-HARD" eye, ↓VA, N/V, severe pain, FIXED MID-DILATED PUPIL, HAZY CORNEA (↓VA due to corneal edema, halos around light)
    • Tx: urgent ophth. ref. → BBs, α-agonist, carb. anhydr. inhib.
  • OCULAR TRAUMA
    • Refer to ophtho: intraocular foreign body, HYPHEMA, medial eyelid lacerations, peaked pupil (iris prolapse), +ve SEIDEL SIGN (penetrating corneal trauma)

nodes.title: Non-Vision Threatening (Red eyes)
nodes.body:
• BLEPHARITIS: chronic eyelid inflamm. causing "dandruff-like" scales
  • STYES: bacterial infection at eyelids. Painful. Tx w. warm compress. Refer if >4 wks.
  • CHALAZION: blocked oil glands at eyelids. Painless. Tx w. warm compress. Refer if persistent.
  • ENTROPION: inward eyelid → lashes abrade cornea. Tx: refer for Sx correction.
  • VIRAL CONJUNCTIVITIS: recent URTI → hyperaemia, CHEMOSIS (conjunctiva blister), lymphadenopathy, normal VA + IOP. Highly CONTAGIOUS. Tx: self-resolves, ↓ spread.
  • BACTERIAL CONJUNCTIVITIS: eyelids w. MUCOPURULENT discharge, CRUSTING + sticky. No photophobia or pruritis, normal VA, no Hx of STI. Most commonly caused by STAPH AUREUS ❗. Tx: most are self-limiting + acute. If not: FLUOROQUINOLONE.
  • GONOCOCCAL CONJUNCTIVITIS: severe purulent discharge and HYPERACUTE onset (12-24 hrs). Tx: refer to ophtho if suspected GONORRHEA or CHLAMYDIA. Ceftriaxone + azithrom. Tx sexual partners w. oral ABx.
  • ALLERGIC CONJUNCTIVITIS: red puffy eyes, OCULAR PRURITIS, sneezing, rhinorrhea. Tx w. antihistamines or mast cell stabilizer drops.
  • SUBCONJUNCTIVAL HEMORRHAGE: trauma, vomiting, valsalva, anticoags → rupture BVs. Tx: reassurance. Benign + self-limiting.
  • CORNEAL ABRASIONS: foreign body sens., blurry vision. Epithelial defect stains w. fluorescein but -ve SEIDEL SIGN (∴ no leakage / full penetration). Tx: ABx drops. If contact lens: FLUOROQUINOLONE.
